By means of great compassion, because he does not abandon suffering beings, his application is directed toward saṃsāra for the sake of others, yet he does not abide in nirvana, like one belonging to the lineage of the vehicle of solitary peace.
Thus, these two factors are the root and the foundation of unsurpassed enlightenment.
Having severed attachment to the self entirely through wisdom, the compassionate one does not attain peace due to his affection for sentient beings;
thus relying upon both wisdom and compassion as the means to enlightenment, the noble one resorts neither to the conventional world nor to extinction.
In this regard, what is shown by the subsequent half-verse concerning the subject of karma previously discussed?
"If the Buddha-element did not exist, there would be no weariness with suffering; nor would there be desire, aspiration, or even the vow for liberation. (40)
And so it has been said:
"Blessed One, if the *tathāgatagarbha* did not exist, there would be no weariness with suffering, nor any desire, longing, or aspiration for *nirvāṇa*.
In this regard, in brief, the lineage (*gotra*) that is the purity of the Buddha-element (*buddhadhātu*) brings about two kinds of effects even for those sentient beings fixed in falsehood.
Based on the observation of the faults and suffering of *saṃsāra*, one generates revulsion;
and based on the observation of the benefits and bliss of *nirvāṇa*, one engenders desire,
aspiration, and resolve.
*Ichā* is the absence of hesitation in the attainment of a desired object.
*Prārthanā* is the searching for the means to attain a desired object.
*Praṇidhi* is the volition (*cetanā*) directed toward a desired object, which is the mental formation (*cittābhisaṃskāra*).

The observation of existence and nirvāṇa, as well as their respective suffering and happiness, faults and virtues, occurs when the spiritual lineage (gotra) exists; it does not exist for those who lack the lineage.

Furthermore, that perception of the faults and suffering in saṃsāra and the perception of the benefits and happiness in nirvāṇa occurs only when the lineage (gotra) of a person possessing the white portion exists; it is neither without cause nor without condition.

For if it were to exist without that lineage—being causeless and conditionless through the application of the total eradication of evil—it would also occur for the Icchantikas who lack the lineage for parinirvāṇa.

And it does not come into being as long as the lineage for the purification of adventitious defilements does not bring about resolute conviction in any one of the three [vehicles], through the application of the encounter with the four white [qualities] beginning with association with holy persons.
For it is said therein:

"Thereafter, even upon the bodies of those beings whose mental continuums are fixed in falsehood, the rays from the solar orb of the Tathāgata fall, in order to generate the causes for the future. (Rgv)
And they cause [beings] to flourish through wholesome qualities.

Furthermore, as for that which was said—that an icchantika is of a nature never to attain parinirvāṇa—that was stated with a view toward a different time (kālāntarābhiprāyeṇa) in order to turn back hostility toward the Mahāyāna teachings; for hostility toward the Mahāyāna teachings is the cause of being an icchantika.
Indeed, no one can possibly be of an absolutely impure nature simply because of the existence of the naturally pure lineage (*prakṛtiviśuddhagotra*).
For this reason, the Blessed One, intending to refer to the capacity for purification present in all sentient beings without distinction, has said:
"Though it is beginningless, it has an end; it is pure by nature and endowed with eternal qualities."
Enveloped on the outside by beginningless sheaths, it is not seen, just like a golden image that has been completely covered.
Regarding that, there is a verse concerning the meaning of "yoga":
Like a great ocean, it is an inexhaustible mine of jewels of immeasurable qualities;
like a lamp, its nature is endowed with inseparable qualities. (42)
In this regard, what is shown by the first half-verse?

By means of the inclusion of the elements of the Dharma-body, the Victor’s gnosis, and compassion, the similarity of this [Buddha-nature] to the ocean through the vessel, the jewel, and the water is demonstrated. (43)

The meaning of "yoga" (union) should be understood with reference to the possession of the cause of the *tathāgata*-element by means of a threefold similarity to the great ocean, corresponding respectively to three points.
What are these three points?
They are as follows: the cause for the purification of the *dharmakāya*.
It is the cause for the attainment of the Buddha-knowledge;
it is the cause for the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s great compassion.
In this regard, the cultivation of resolute faith in the Mahāyāna should be seen as the cause for the purification of the Dharma-body.
The cultivation of the gateways of wisdom and meditative concentration is the cause for the attainment of the Buddha’s gnosis;
the cultivation of the compassion of a bodhisattva is the cause for the arising of the great compassion of a Tathāgata.

In this regard, the cultivation of faith in the Mahāyāna shares the common characteristic of being a vessel, because within it there is the convergence of the waters of immeasurable, inexhaustible jewels of wisdom, meditative concentration, and compassion.
The cultivation of the gateway of wisdom and meditative concentration shares the commonality with a jewel because it is non-conceptual and possesses qualities of inconceivable power.
The cultivation of a bodhisattva’s compassion shares the commonality with water because its application is characterized by a single flavor of supreme tenderness toward all living beings.
The conjunction (*yoga*) consisting of the possession of these three factors through these three types of causes is what is called "endowment" (*samanvāgama*).
In this regard, what does the latter half-verse demonstrate?
"Because of the non-separation of the superknowledges, knowledge, purity, and suchness, there is a similarity with the light, heat, and color of a lamp in the immaculate basis. (44)

The meaning of "yoga" should be understood with respect to the possession of the fruit by the *tathāgatadhātu*, by means of a threefold similarity to a lamp corresponding respectively to three points.
What are these three points?
They are as follows:
The superknowledges (*abhijñā*) consist of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) and the destruction of the outflows itself (*āsravakṣaya*).

Among these, the five superknowledges possess the common characteristic of a flame, because their defining characteristic is being present as the dispeller of the darkness that is the adversary to the knowledge that experiences objects.

The knowledge of the destruction of the outflows possesses the common characteristic of heat, because its defining characteristic is being present as the burner of the fuel of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) without remainder.

The transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) shares the same quality as the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) in terms of its color, because it is characterized by being absolutely stainless, pure, and luminous.
In this context, it is "stainless" (*vimala*) due to the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
and "pure" (*viśuddha*) due to the abandonment of the obscuration to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It is luminous by nature because both of those [defilements] are adventitious.

Thus, in brief, the mutual inseparability and non-distinctness of these seven factors— comprised of superknowledges, gnosis, and abandonments— which belong to the continuum of one beyond training within the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), is called "endowment," "possession," or "union" with the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
And this simile of the lamp, concerning the meaning of yoga, is to be understood in detail according to the sūtra:
"For example, Śāriputra, a lamp consists of inseparable dharmas."
It is not separated from its qualities;
that is to say, as light is inseparable from its heat and color,
or as a jewel is inseparable from its light, color, and shape.

In the same way, Śāriputra, the *dharmakāya* taught by the Tathāgata is of an inseparable nature, not dissociated from the qualities of wisdom—namely, the qualities of a Tathāgata that exceed the sands of the river Gaṅgā. Regarding the meaning of its manifestation therein, there is this verse: "Because suchness is not distinct among ordinary beings, noble ones, and the perfectly awakened Buddhas..."
This *jigarbha* among sentient beings has been taught by those who perceive reality. // 45 //
What is shown by this?

Ordinary beings are subject to error; those who have seen the truth are the opposite [of that]; and the Tathāgatas, being free from conceptual proliferation, are non-erroneous in accordance with reality. (46)

That is to say, this common characteristic of the purity of the suchness of all phenomena of the *tathāgata*-element (*tathāgatadhātu*), which has been taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other scriptures beginning with the instruction on the gateway of non-conceptual knowledge, concerns, in brief, three types of persons among bodhisattvas:
the ordinary person who does not see reality, the noble one who sees reality, and the *tathāgata* who has reached the culmination of purity.
The threefold division of activity should be understood as follows:
namely, that which is perverted, that which is non-perverted, and that which is correctly non-perverted and free from conceptual proliferation, respectively.
In this regard, for the foolish, perception, mind, and view are inverted due to the inversion of perception, mind, and view;
for the noble ones, they are non-inverted by virtue of the opposite, through the abandonment of those [inversions];

and for the perfectly awakened ones, they are correctly non-inverted and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) because of the total eradication of the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*).
From this point onward, beginning with this very [topic] for the sake of its exposition, the other four topics are to be understood through their detailed classification alone.
In that regard, concerning the distinction between the stages of these three types of persons, there is a verse:
"Impure, impure-pure, and then perfectly pure, respectively."
That which is called the realm of sentient beings is the bodhisattva, the Tathāgata. // 47 //
What is shown by this? In brief, the element (dhātu), through these six meanings beginning with "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) and so forth, is known by three names throughout its three states. (48)

Thus, whatever detailed explanations of the outflow-free realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) have been taught by the Blessed One through various gateways of Dharma-discourses, all of them should be understood as being subsumed, in brief, within these very six topics— essence, cause, fruit, activity, endowment, and manifestation— and as being taught according to their respective order through the designation of three names across three stages.
That is to say: in the impure state, it is called the *sattvadhātu*;
in the impure-pure state, it is called a *bodhisattva*;
and in the perfectly pure state, it is called a *tathāgata*.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"Śāriputra, this very Dharmakāya, when concealed within the sheaths of limitless afflictions,

carried along by the stream of saṃsāra, and wandering through deaths and births in the various realms of existence throughout beginningless and endless saṃsāra, is called the 'realm of sentient beings'."

Śāriputra, that very same *dharmakāya*, when weary of the suffering of the stream of *saṃsāra* and detached from all objects of sensual desire, practicing the conduct for the sake of awakening through the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma contained within the ten *pāramitās*, is called a "Bodhisattva. Furthermore, Śāriputra, that very same *dharmakāya*, when completely liberated from the sheath of all afflictions and having transcended all suffering—

Free from all secondary afflictions and impurities, pure, utterly purified, and abiding in the supremely pure nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he has ascended to the stage that is to be beheld by all sentient beings; having attained the peerless human power over the entire range of the knowable, and having realized the state of unobstructed mastery over all phenomena through the power of unhindered qualities, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Regarding the all-pervading nature of the *tathāgata*-element throughout those same three states, there is this verse:
"Just as space, which is non-conceptual by nature, is omnipresent everywhere, so too is the element of the stainless nature of the mind omnipresent. (49)
What is demonstrated by this?
Its general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) pervades [all] the defects, virtues, and culminations, just as space pervades forms that are inferior, middling, or superior. (50)

That nature of the non-conceptual mind belonging to ordinary beings, noble ones, and perfectly awakened Buddhas—being a universal characteristic—is, like space, present at all times, following and entering into the three states in their respective order: even amidst faults, even amidst virtues, and even in the culmination of the purification of virtues; it is equal, undifferentiated, and attained at all times.
For this very reason, immediately after the explanation of the states, he says:
"Therefore, Śāriputra, the realm of sentient beings is not other than the Dharma-body;
the Dharma-body is none other than the realm of sentient beings."
The realm of sentient beings is indeed the *dharmakāya*;
these two are non-dual in meaning,
differing only in their verbal expression.

Regarding these very three states, there are fourteen verses concerning the fact that although the *tathāgata*-element is omnipresent, it remains immutable through both its defilement and purification. Furthermore, their summarized meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) should be understood as follows:
"Because of the association with adventitious defects, and because of the association with the nature of qualities."
As it was before, so it is after; such is the nature of phenomena, which is unchanging.

By means of thirteen verses— twelve verses for the impure state and the impure-pure state respectively, and the fourteenth verse for the perfectly pure state— the nature of the Tathāgata-element is elucidated as being absolutely immutable throughout its prior and subsequent stages. This is because, in the impure and impure-pure states, it is conjoined with adventitious defects of primary and secondary afflictions, whereas in the perfectly pure state, it is conjoined by nature with the inconceivable Buddha-qualities— which exceed the sands of the river Gaṅgā in number, are inseparable [from it], and are never abandoned— just as the element of space is conjoined with its own nature.
In that regard, concerning the meaning of "unchangeability" starting from the impure state, what are the twelve verses?
"Just as space, because of its subtlety, is not defiled though it is omnipresent, so this [nature], though abiding everywhere within sentient beings, is likewise not defiled. (52)
Just as space undergoes both increase and decrease everywhere for all people, so too do the arising and passing away of the faculties occur within the unconditioned realm. // 53 //
Just as the sky has never before been burned by fires,
so too do the fires of death, disease, and old age not consume him.
Earth is established in water, water in air, and air is established in space;
yet space is not established in the elements of air, water, or earth.
In the same way, the aggregates, elements, and sense-faculties are established upon karma and afflictions;
karma and afflictions are always established upon improper mental attention. (56)
Improper mental attention is established upon the purity of the mind;
yet the nature of the mind with respect to all phenomena is non-abiding. (57)
The aggregates, sense-bases, and elements should be known as being like the earth element;
the karma and afflictions of embodied beings should be known as resembling the water element. (58)
Improper mental attention should be understood as being like the wind element;
its nature is rootless and without foundation, like the space element. (59)
Improper mental activity adheres to the nature of the mind;
afflictions and karma arise from improper mental attention. (60)
The aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, produced by the waters of karma and afflictions, arise and cease like the processes of cosmic dissolution and evolution. (61)
The nature of the mind, like the element of space, has no cause, nor condition, nor causal totality, nor arising; it has neither cessation nor abiding.
That nature of the mind which is luminous never undergoes transformation, just like the sky;
however, it undergoes defilement through adventitious stains such as passion, which arise from unreal conceptualization. (63)
How is the unchanging nature (*avikāradharmatā*) of the *tathāgata*-element in its impure state illustrated by this analogy of space?
It is said:
"The accumulation of the waters of karma and afflictions does not bring it into being."
Even when fully ablaze, the fires of death, disease, and old age do not consume it.

Just as the world of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields— which arises in dependence upon the mass of water consisting of karma and afflictions produced by the whirlwind of improper mental attention— does not cause the destruction of the space-element that is the nature of the mind; likewise, even though the mass of fire consisting of death, sickness, and old age arises for the sake of the disappearance of the world of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields established upon the wind and water masses of improper mental attention, karma, and afflictions, it does not cause the dissolution of that [nature].
It should be understood that, in this way,

even though there is the arising and passing away of the entire defilement of afflictions, karma, and birth— just like the receptacle world— in the impure state, the unconditioned *tathāgata*-element, being like space, is shown to be of an absolutely immutable nature due to its non-arising and non-cessation.
And this analogy of space, beginning with the gateway to the light of the Dharma called the gateway to natural purity, is to be understood in detail according to the sūtra:
"Friends, the afflictions are darkness;
light is purity."
The afflictions are weak;
insight is powerful;
the afflictions are adventitious.
The fundamental nature is pure by its very root;
the afflictions are conceptual constructions;
the fundamental nature is non-conceptual.
For example, friends, this great earth is established upon water;
the water is established upon wind;
and the wind is established upon space.

And space is non-abiding. Thus, among these four elements— the earth element, the water element, the wind element, and the space element— it is the space element alone that is powerful, firm, immovable, without increase, without decrease, unarisen, unceasing, and remains by its own inherent nature.
In this regard, those three elements are characterized by arising and ceasing; they are unstable and do not endure for long.
A transformation of these is observed, but there is no transformation whatsoever of the space element.
In the very same way, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are established upon karma and afflictions.
Karma and afflictions are established upon improper mental attention;
improper mental attention is established upon the natural purity [of the mind].
Therefore, it is said that the mind, which is luminous by nature, is defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions.

In that regard, whatever improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) there is subsequently, whatever karmic afflictions (*karmakleśa*), and whatever aggregates, elements, and sense-fields (*skandhadhātvāyatana*)— all these phenomena arise gathered through causes and conditions, and they cease through the disjunction of causes and conditions.
Furthermore, as for that intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*), it has no cause, no condition, no collection [of causes and conditions], no arising, and no cessation.
In this regard, as is the element of space, so is intrinsic nature;
as is the element of wind, so is improper mental attention;
as is the element of water, so are karma and the afflictions.
Just as it is with the earth element, so it is with the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Therefore, it is said that all phenomena have a root that is without essence, a root that is without foundation, a pure root, and a root that is rootless.

Thus, regarding the impure state, the similarity of the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) to the space element has been explained, as well as that of the improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) which relies upon it.
Regarding the characteristics of the causes of karma and afflictions, their similarity to the wind element and the water element has been explained;
regarding the ripening characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases produced from those [causes], their similarity to the earth element has been explained;

however, the similarity to the fire element—starting from the characteristics of the calamities of the fires of death, sickness, and old age which are the causes for the dissolution of those [aggregates]—has not yet been stated, and so it is now said:
At the end of the eon, there are three fires: the hellish fire, the natural fire, and the fire [of destruction] respectively;
death, disease, and old age are the three fires that serve as their analogues.
The similarity between fire and death, illness, and old age should be understood through three causes, respectively:

by way of making the six sense-bases free from the sense of "mine," by way of experiencing various types of suffering, and by way of bringing about the maturation of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, with regard to the immutability [of the Tathāgata-element] even amidst these fires of death, illness, and old age, this was said concerning its impure state.
“Worldly convention, O Blessed One, speaks of one as ‘dead’ or as ‘born.
“O Blessed One, ‘dead’ refers to the cessation of the sense faculties;
‘born,’ O Blessed One, refers to the manifestation of new sense faculties.”
"O Blessed One, the *tathāgatagarbha* is neither born, nor does it age, nor does it die, nor does it pass away, nor is it reborn.
For what reason?
Because, O Blessed One, the *tathāgatagarbha* transcends the domain of conditioned characteristics; it is eternal, stable, quiescent, and immutable."
In that regard, concerning the state of being both impure and pure, there is a verse beginning with the meaning of "unchanging":

"Having realized the very nature of this [reality] as it truly is, without alteration—[a nature] free from birth, cessation, sickness, and old age—the wise, though free from the calamities of birth and so forth, engage in the world out of the arising of compassion for its sake. (66)
What does this demonstrate?
The Noble Ones have uprooted the root of suffering—death, sickness, and old age.
Birth occurs through the power of karma and afflictions; since those do not exist for them, birth does not occur in them. (67)

Indeed, for this fire of death, sickness, and old age in its impure state, birth—preceded by improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), karma, and afflictions (*kleśa*)—serves as the fuel, like the material cause (*upādāna*).
Because it does not appear at all in those Bodhisattvas who have attained a mind-made body (*manomayātmabhāva*) during their pure-impure state, the absolute non-blazing of that [fire] is recognized.
Those whose nature is compassion manifest birth, death, old age, and sickness.
And they have turned away from birth and so forth through the vision of things as they truly are. // 68 //
For, through their connection with the roots of virtue and by relying on the mastery of intentional rebirth, Bodhisattvas, out of compassion, remain attached to the triple world;
they manifest birth, and they even manifest old age, sickness, and death.
Yet, these phenomena of birth and so forth do not actually exist for them.
This is because one sees, as it truly is, the non-arising and non-origination of this very realm (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, this stage of the bodhisattva is to be understood in detail according to the sūtra,
as it says:

And what are those afflictions associated with the roots of virtue that set saṃsāra in motion? Namely: insatiability in seeking the accumulation of merit, and the intentional taking up of rebirth in existence.
The aspiration to meet with the Buddhas;
tirelessness in maturing sentient beings;
and exertion in upholding the true Dharma.
Eagerness for what must be done for the sake of sentient beings;
not relinquishing the latent tendency toward passion for the Dharma;
and not abandoning the fetters of the perfections.
Thus, Sāgaramati, these are the afflictions associated with roots of virtue, by which bodhisattvas are bound;
yet they are certainly not defiled by the faults of the afflictions.
Furthermore, he said:
"Blessed One, for what reason are roots of virtue called 'afflictions'?
He replied,
"Sāgaramati, it is because by means of such afflictions as these, bodhisattvas become attached to the triple world."
And the triple world arises from the afflictions (*kleśa*).
In that regard, through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) and by the application of the power of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*), Bodhisattvas intentionally adhere to the triple world.
Therefore, they are called "afflictions associated with the roots of virtue."
It is only by way of attachment to the triple world, and not by way of mental affliction.

Sāgaramati, it is just as if, for example, the only son of a merchant householder were beloved, charming, dear, pleasing, and not disagreeable to behold; yet that boy, while dancing about in his childishness, might fall into a pit of excrement.
Then, suppose the mother and kinsmen of that boy were to see him fallen into the pit of filth;
having seen him, they would sigh deeply, grieve, and lament,
yet they would not descend into that pit of filth [to rescue him].
They would be clinging to that child.
Then the father of that child would come to that place;

seeing his only son fallen into a cesspool, and having seen him, he—impelled by the intense love and affection for his only son, acting with great haste and speed, and feeling no disgust—would descend into that cesspool and lift his only son out.
Thus, Sāgaramati, this analogy has been made solely for the sake of making the meaning known.
What is the underlying connection to be seen?
"A cesspool," Sāgaramati, is a designation for the triple world.
"One only son" is a designation for sentient beings;
for a bodhisattva’s perception of all sentient beings as an only son is ever-present.

"Maternal kinsmen" is a designation for those persons belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who, seeing sentient beings fallen into saṃsāra, grieve and lament, yet are not capable of [rescuing them].
They are able to lift it up.

"Merchant" and "householder" are designations for a bodhisattva who is pure, stainless, and of immaculate mind, who has attained direct realization of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), yet intentionally takes rebirth within the triple world for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
Sāgaramati, this is the great compassion of a bodhisattva: that though he is utterly liberated from all bonds, he nevertheless takes up rebirth in existence;
and being embraced by skillful means and wisdom, he is not defiled by the afflictions, yet he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings for the sake of abandoning all bonds of the afflictions.

Thus, by this explanation of the scriptural passage, the state that is both impure and pure is illuminated: for a Bodhisattva who has mastery over the performance of the welfare of others, through the conjunction of the power of roots of virtue and compassion with intentional rebirth in existence, and through the powers of skillful means and wisdom, there is no defilement therein.

In this regard, when a Bodhisattva, having attained the vision of non-arising and non-origination as it truly is, reaches this nature of a Bodhisattva within the *tathāgata*-element, it should be understood in detail according to the Sūtra.

As it says: "Behold, Sāgaramati, the insubstantiality, the lack of agency, the selflessness, the absence of a sentient being, the absence of a living soul, the absence of a person, and the lack of ownership of all phenomena."
For indeed, Sāgaramati, when things are manifested exactly as they are intended, and having been so manifested, they neither conceptualize nor construct;
by being resolved upon this manifestation of phenomena (*dharmaviṭhapanā*), a bodhisattva does not give rise to weariness toward any phenomenon whatsoever.
His very vision of knowledge becomes pure and stainless.
"No benefit or harm whatsoever is being done here"—
thus he understands the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as it really is;
and yet, in this way, he does not abandon the armor of great compassion (mahākaruṇā).

Sāgaramati, it is as if, for example, there were a priceless *vaiḍūrya* jewel—well-polished, perfectly pure, and stainless—that had been cast into mud and remained there for a thousand years. After the passing of those thousand years, it were to be lifted out from that mud, scrubbed, and thoroughly cleansed. Once it has been well-washed, purified, and completely cleansed, it would not abandon its very nature as a pure and stainless jewel.
In the same way, Sāgaramati, a bodhisattva understands that the nature of the minds of sentient beings is luminous;
yet he perceives that it is defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions.
In this regard, the bodhisattva thinks as follows:
"These afflictions have not entered into the luminous nature of the minds of sentient beings;
these afflictions are adventitious, arisen from unreal conceptualization.
May I be able to teach the Dharma to remove these adventitious afflictions from these sentient beings."
Thus, no thought of discouragement arises in him; rather,
to an even greater degree, a thought of liberation toward all sentient beings arises within him,
and he thinks as follows:
These afflictions possess no strength or power whatsoever;
these afflictions are weak and feeble. They have no real foundation at all.
These afflictions are falsely imagined;
when scrutinized through correct and thorough mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*) as they truly are, they do not provoke anger.
We should examine them in such a way that they no longer adhere to us.
For non-attachment to the afflictions is beneficial for a practitioner, but attachment is not.
If I were to become attached to the afflictions, how could I teach the Dharma for the sake of severing the bonds of affliction for those beings who are bound by the fetters of affliction?
Come now, we shall neither be attached to the afflictions, nor shall we fail to teach the Dharma to beings for the sake of severing the bonds of affliction.
Furthermore, regarding those afflictions associated with the wholesome that bind one to the continuity of saṃsāra, we should adhere to them for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
Moreover, "saṃsāra" here refers to the three bodies made of mind within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), which are reflections of the triple world.
Because they are produced by untainted roots of virtue, it is called "saṃsāra."
Because it is not conditioned by outflowing karma and afflictions, even nirvāṇa is that [saṃsāra].
With reference to this, it was said:
"Therefore, Blessed One, there is a saṃsāra that is both conditioned and unconditioned."
There is a nirvāṇa that is both conditioned and unconditioned.
In that regard, because it is associated with the activity of the mind and mental factors that are intermingled with the conditioned and the unconditioned, this is called the state of impure purity.

Furthermore, through the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom free from attachment, which is oriented toward the superknowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*), and through the cultivation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), [this state is attained].
And for the sake of protecting the realm of all sentient beings, because that [knowledge] has not yet been directly realized, it is established primarily on the Bodhisattva stage called Ābhimukhī.
This is illustrated by the analogy of the city, beginning with the aforementioned knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*):

"In the same way, noble son, through mental discipline, great effort, great vigor, and the practice of firm resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), the bodhisattva generates the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*)."

For one whose mind has been prepared through the cultivation of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) becomes manifest.

Through the arousal of the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for the sake of protecting all sentient beings, and having mastered the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, he once again— his mind thoroughly prepared— becomes manifest in the destruction of the outflows due to the arising of unimpeded wisdom (*asaṅgaprajñā*) on the sixth stage.
Thus, in this *Abhimukhī* bodhisattva stage, the state of purity of the bodhisattva who has attained mastery over the realization of the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is elucidated.
For him who has thus correctly practiced himself, there arises the thought: "I shall establish others as well in this very same correct practice."

For one whose intention is to protect beings who have fallen into error through great compassion; who, by not relishing the bliss of tranquility, has mastered the means for that purpose; who, out of regard for beings facing toward cyclic existence, turns away from nirvana; and who, having dwelt in the meditative absorptions to fulfill the factors of enlightenment, intentionally takes rebirth in the desire realm as long as he wishes to act for the benefit of sentient beings.
The impure state is illustrated by the attainment of mastery in manifesting the physical forms of ordinary beings through various types of birth stories (*jātaka*) among the diverse animal realms.
This is another meaning of the verse.

Having discerned this unchanging nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the Son of the Victor perceives that which is seen by those blinded by ignorance amidst birth and so forth—that is truly marvelous. (69)

Therefore, although the Friend of the World possesses supreme skillful means and compassion, he is seen within the sphere of ordinary beings even though he has attained the sphere of the noble ones. (70)
He has transcended all worlds, yet he has not departed from the world; he moves within the world for the sake of the world, unstained by worldly defilements. // 71 //
Just as a lotus born in the water is not defiled by the water,
so too he, though born in the world, is not defiled by worldly conditions.
His intellect is eternally blazing like fire in the accomplishment of its tasks, yet he is always engaged in the attainment of peaceful meditative absorption. // 73 //
Due to the force of previous momentum and because of the departure of all conceptual constructions, he no longer exerts effort for the sake of maturing embodied beings. (74)

In whatever way, by whatever means, and in whatever manner a person to be trained is perceived, in that very way [the Buddha] appears through teaching, through the form-body, through conduct, or through deportment. (75)
Thus, for him whose intellect is always unimpeded, the welfare of sentient beings proceeds effortlessly throughout the world as far as the limits of space. (76)
Having attained this state, the Bodhisattva attains equality with the Tathāgatas regarding the crossing over of sentient beings in the worlds. (77)
Furthermore, the difference between a Bodhisattva and a Buddha is like the difference between a mustard seed and the earth, or between the water in a cow’s footprint and the great ocean. (78)

By means of nine of these ten verses in their respective order, the extreme degree of affliction below the Bodhisattva stage of *Pramuditā* is established, and by the tenth verse, the extreme degree of purity above the Bodhisattva stage of *Dharmameghā* is established;
thus, in brief, the purity and impurity of the four types of Bodhisattvas across the ten Bodhisattva stages are fully illuminated.
There are four types of bodhisattvas: those who have first generated the mind of awakening, those who have entered into the practice, and those who are irreversible.
Regarding the term "bound to one more birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*):

therein, by means of the first and second verses, the characteristic of the purity of the assembly of bodhisattvas who have first generated the thought of awakening on the *pramuditā* stage is elucidated, due to their penetration of the supramundane reality (*dharmatā*) that has never been seen before throughout beginningless time.

By means of the third and fourth verses, the characteristic of the purity of the qualities of bodhisattvas engaged in practice— from the Vimalā stage up to the Adūraṃgamā stage— is elucidated through their performance of conduct that is undefiled. By the fifth verse, the characteristic of the purity of the qualities of irreversible bodhisattvas on the Acalā stage is elucidated, owing to their establishment in the meditative concentrations of the uninterrupted application for the attainment of great awakening.

By the sixth, seventh, and eighth verses, the characteristic of the purification of the qualities of a bodhisattva bound to one more birth on the Bodhisattva stage called Dharmameghā is elucidated; for one who has reached the culmination of the means for accomplishing all the welfare of oneself and others is connected to the Buddha-stage by only one final birth, thereby attaining unsurpassed, supreme perfect enlightenment.

By the ninth and tenth verses, the lack of distinction and the distinction between the purity of qualities of the Bodhisattva who has reached the culmination and the Tathāgata are elucidated, beginning with the welfare of others and the welfare of oneself. In that regard, concerning the meaning of immutability in the state of perfect purity, there is this verse: "Because it possesses inexhaustible qualities whose nature is non-alteration, the Refuge of the world remains so until the limit of the future."
This [reality] is eternally non-dual because it is free from conceptual construction; it is of an indestructible nature because its essence is uncreated. // 79 //
What does this demonstrate?
It neither is born, nor dies, is awakened, nor decays;
because it is eternal, stable, auspicious, and permanent. (80)
He is not born because of his eternity through mind-made bodies;
he does not die because of his steadfastness through inconceivable transformation. (81)

It is not afflicted by the subtle diseases of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) because it is of the nature of auspiciousness (*śivatva*); it does not decay through untainted formative forces (*anāsrava-abhisaṃskāra*) because it is eternal (*śāśvata*). // 82 //

Friend, this Tathāgata, abiding in his own nature—which is the stage of a Buddha characterized by ultimate stainlessness, purity, and luminosity—is not born again through mind-made bodies because he is eternal from the perspective of the prior limit; nor does he die again through the inconceivable transformation-death because he is constant from the perspective of the posterior limit;
nor is he afflicted again by the grasping of the ground of the latency of ignorance because he is auspicious from the perspective of both the prior and posterior limits.
And he who has thus fallen into such a state of non-adversity does not age again through the transformation of the fruit of untainted karma, because of his permanence.
In that regard, the meaning of permanence and so forth in the unconditioned state is to be understood by means of two, then two, two, and two words respectively. (83)

Therefore, regarding these four terms— eternal (*nitya*), stable (*dhruva*), auspicious (*śiva*), and constant (*śāśvata*)— within the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*), the differentiation of the meaning of each single term should be understood according to the sūtra through two pairs of terms consisting of a brief statement (*uddeśa*) and an explanation (*nirdeśa*). As it is said:

Śāriputra, this dharmakāya is eternal because its nature is non-dual and inexhaustible; Śāriputra, this dharmakāya is stable because it is a stable refuge through its equality with the ultimate limit; Śāriputra, this dharmakāya is auspicious because its nature is non-dual and free from conceptual construction.
"Śāriputra, this Dharmakāya is eternal because it is of an indestructible nature and an unconditioned nature.

Regarding this very state of purity, there is a verse concerning the non-differentiation of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is characterized by the attainment of the ultimate limit of absolute purification:
"That is the Dharmakāya; that is the Tathāgata; therefore, it is the Noble Truth and the Nirvāṇa of the ultimate meaning."
Therefore, there is no nirvāṇa apart from Buddhahood, because its qualities are inseparable, like the rays of the sun. // 84 //
In this regard, what does the first half of the verse demonstrate?

"In brief, the synonyms such as the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) and so forth should be understood as fourfold within the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu), according to the distinction of four meanings. (85)

In brief, with reference to four meanings within the immaculate realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) of the *tathāgatagarbha*, four synonymous designations are to be understood. What are these four meanings? They are:
the inseparability of the Buddha-qualities [from that realm], the arrival at the state of suchness (*tathāgama*) of that lineage (*gotra*), and so forth.
The nature of being non-deceptive and non-delusive, and primordial quiescence from the very beginning. // 86 //
The meaning is the inseparability from the Buddha-qualities (buddhadharma). With reference to this, it was said:
"O Blessed One, the tathāgatagarbha is not empty; it is endowed with Buddha-qualities that exceed the sands of the river Gaṅgā in number, which are inseparable, non-released, and inconceivable."

This refers to the meaning of the attainment of the lineage's nature (*prakṛti*) in an inconceivable manner; with reference to this, it was said: "That particularity of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana-viśeṣa*) is such that it has been transmitted through succession, is beginningless, and is obtained as the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)."
The meaning of "non-deceptive" (amṛṣā) is as follows; with reference to this it was said: "In that regard, ultimate truth is that which has the nature of being non-deceptive, namely, nirvāṇa."
For what reason?
Because that lineage is eternal by virtue of its uniform nature;
this refers to the sense of ultimate quiescence.
With reference to this, it was said: "The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is from the very beginning parinirvṛta—unborn and unceasing.
Regarding these four meanings, there are these four synonymous designations in their respective order.
Namely, that the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and *nirvāṇa*. For it has been said:
"Śāriputra, 'Tathāgatagarbha' is a designation for the *dharmakāya*."
“O Blessed One, the Tathāgata is not one thing and the Dharmakāya another; O Blessed One, the Dharmakāya itself is the Tathāgata.
O Blessed One, it is by the name ‘the cessation of suffering’ that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, endowed with such qualities, has been taught.”
"O Blessed One, 'the realm of nirvāṇa' is a designation for the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
In that regard, what does the other half-verse demonstrate?
"The complete awakening in all its aspects, together with the uprooting of the enemy along with its latent impressions."
Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, Buddhahood and Nirvana are non-dual. // 87 //

Since these four synonyms for the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*) converge upon this single, indivisible reality that is the *tathāgatadhātu*, they possess a single meaning. Therefore, by way of the principle of non-duality, both that which is called "awakening" (*buddhatva*)— due to the perfect awakening to all phenomena in all their aspects— and that which is called "nirvāṇa"— due to the great perfect awakening and the abandonment of stains along with their residual impressions (*savāsanā*)— are non-dual within the untainted realm.
It should be seen as undifferentiated and uninterrupted;
by means of all modes, it is characterized by qualities that are incalculable, inconceivable, and stainless.
Liberation is of an undifferentiated nature; that which is liberation is the Tathāgata.
As for what was said concerning the parinirvāṇa of arhats and pratyekabuddhas—
"O Bhagavat, 'nirvāṇa' is a skillful means of the Tathāgatas"—

by this it is illustrated that, like the conjuring of a city in the middle of a wilderness for those exhausted by a long journey, this is a skillful means for non-retrogression employed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the supreme lords of Dharma.

“O Blessed One, through the attainment of nirvāṇa, the Tathāgatas become Arhats, perfectly enlightened ones, endowed with all qualities that have reached the ultimate limit of immeasurable and inconceivable purity.

By this it is shown that, having attained nirvāṇa— which is characterized by the non-distinction of the perfection of qualities in its four aspects— the perfectly enlightened ones come to have that as their very nature.
It is demonstrated that because Buddhahood and Nirvāṇa are endowed with inseparable qualities, there is no attainment of Nirvāṇa for anyone apart from Buddhahood.

In that regard, within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) of the Tathāgatas, the universality of qualities (*guṇasarvatā*) should be understood through the analogy of a painter, by virtue of the manifestation of emptiness endowed with the excellence of all modes.
Just as there might be painters who are mutually skilled [in their respective parts],...
Whoever should understand a particular limb, another should not grasp it. // 88 //
Then the powerful king shall grant a reward to them by his command:
"By all of you here, a service must be rendered to me. (89)
Then, having given him his word, they should apply themselves to the work of painting;
among those engaged there, one should go to another land. (90)
When he has gone to another land, that image, due to separation from him, would not be complete in all its parts; thus was the simile made. (91)
The scribes who possess those forms—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and so forth—are described as emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects. (92)

In this regard, it should be understood that each one of these [perfections], such as generosity and the rest, is immeasurable because it is divided into infinite varieties within the domain of the Buddhas;
it is inconceivable by virtue of its number and its power;
and it possesses the highest purity because it has eliminated the stains of the latencies of opposing factors such as stinginess.

In that regard, through the cultivation of the gateways of the samādhi of emptiness endowed with the excellence of all modes, and by virtue of attaining the non-arising of phenomena on the Immovable Bodhisattva stage, there arises the totality of qualities within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) of the Tathāgatas, based upon the knowledge of the path that is non-conceptual, unbroken, uninterrupted, and flowing spontaneously.

In the Bodhisattva stage of Sādhumatī, through the support of the knowledge that encompasses immeasurable Buddha-qualities by means of oceans of gates of incalculable samādhis and dhāraṇīs, the immeasurability of qualities is fully realized.
In the Bodhisattva stage of Dharmameghā, through the support of the knowledge that is not obscure regarding the inner abode of all Tathāgatas, the inconceivability of qualities is fully realized.

Immediately thereafter, for the sake of attaining the Buddha-stage, through the support of the knowledge of liberation from all afflictive and cognitive obstructions along with their latent tendencies, the supreme purity of qualities is fully realized.

Because Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are not seen within these four bases of the knowledge of the stages, it is said that they remain distant from the realm of nirvana, which is characterized by the non-differentiation of the perfection of the fourfold qualities. This is due to the brilliance, pervasiveness, and purity of their wisdom, gnosis, and liberation.
And there is similarity by way of non-difference with light, rays, and the solar orb. // 93 //

By means of which wisdom (*prajñā*), which knowledge (*jñāna*), and which liberation (*vimukti*), that realm of *nirvāṇa*—characterized by the non-distinction from the perfection of the fourfold qualities—is indicated; for these, respectively, through three and one cause, a fourfold similarity to the sun is elucidated.

In this regard, the similarity of wisdom to light consists in its presence as the dispeller of the darkness regarding the supreme reality of the knowable, being supramundane and non-conceptual within the continuum of a Buddha.

The wisdom of omniscience attained subsequent to that [meditative concentration] possesses a commonality with the radiation of a web of light rays, because it proceeds toward all objects of knowledge in every aspect without exception.
The liberation of the nature of the mind, which is the basis for both of those, possesses a commonality with the purity of the solar disk, because it is utterly stainless and luminous.
And all three possess a commonality in their inseparability, because they have the undifferentiated nature of the *dharmadhātu* as their essence.
Therefore, without attaining Buddhahood, nirvana is not realized.
For it is not possible to behold the sun while excluding its radiance and rays. // 94 //
Since, in this way, within the element that is naturally endowed with pure qualities through beginningless proximity, there exists the inseparable nature of the qualities of the Tathāgatas,

it is therefore not possible to attain— that is, to realize— the realm of nirvāṇa characterized by liberation from all obscurations without relying upon the state of a Tathāgata, which consists of unattached and unimpeded insight and gnosis; it would be like seeing the orb of the sun without seeing its light and rays.
Therefore, he said this:
"For indeed, Blessed One, there is no attainment of nirvāṇa for those whose dharmas are inferior or superior;
Blessed One, there is the attainment of nirvāṇa for those whose dharmas are equal."
Blessed One, for those who possess equal knowledge, equal liberation, and equal vision and knowledge of liberation, there is the attainment of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, Blessed One, the realm of nirvāṇa is said to be of a single flavor, of an equal flavor; that is to say, by way of the flavor of knowledge and liberation.
Thus, the tenfold state of being the embryo of the Jina has been explained;
furthermore, its nature as an embryo enveloped by the sheath of afflictions should be understood through illustrative examples. (95)

Thus, with reference to the existence of the eternally stable *dharmatā* which reaches the furthest limit of the future, the establishment of the *tathāgatagarbha* has been explained by way of ten meanings. Furthermore, with reference to the nature of the sheaths of afflictions (*kleśakośa*) which have coexisted since beginningless time yet are not inherently connected, and the nature of pure qualities (*śubhadharma*) which have coexisted since beginningless time and are inherently connected,
one should understand— as stated in the Sūtra— that the *tathāgatagarbha* is concealed within the sheaths of limitless millions of afflictions by means of nine illustrations.
What are the nine illustrations?
The Buddha in a withered lotus, honey among bees, kernels within husks, gold in filth;
A treasure in the earth, sprouts and so forth in small fruit, and the body of a Jina in tattered rags. (96)

Just as kingship may exist within the womb of a lowly woman, or a jewel-image within clods of earth, so too does this Element abide within sentient beings who are shrouded by the adventitious stains of afflictions. (97)
The impurities— [likened to] lotuses, bees, husks, chaff, bark, rotten rags, and dross—
are like the earth-element scorched by the flames of the three sufferings;
yet they reveal the Buddha, honey, pure essence, gold, a treasure, a nyagrodha tree, and a jewel.
That supreme relic is like a stainless reflection of the jewel of the Lord of the foremost continent. // 98 //
The afflictions are like the sheaths of withered lotuses;
the *tathāgatadhātu* is like a Buddha.
Just as a Tathāgata, radiant with the thousand marks, might be enclosed within the interior of a discolored lotus, so it is here.
A man with pure, divine vision, having observed it, would release it from the sheath of the lotus petal. // 99 //

In the same way, the Sugata, beholding his own true nature even among those dwelling in the Avīci hell with his Buddha-eye, being himself unobstructed and abiding until the furthest limit of time, liberates them from their obscurations, for he is the very embodiment of compassion. (100)
Just as one with divine vision, seeing a loathsome lotus that has closed up, would cut away its petals upon beholding the Sugata situated within its heart,

so too the Sage, out of compassion, beholds the world— encased in the sheath of the impurities of passion, hatred, and the like— which contains the embryo of a Perfect Buddha, and removes those obstructions. (101)
The afflictions are like small insects,
and the *tathāgata*-element is like honey.
Just as a wise man seeking honey, having observed it covered by a swarm of insects, [proceeds to remove them].
Therefore, one should effect the departure of the multitude of living beings from that place by means of skillful methods on all sides. // 102 //
Having perceived this element, which resembles honey, with the eye of omniscience, the Great Sage brings about the absolute non-attachment of its veils, which resemble bees. (103)
Just as a man seeking honey, having destroyed thousands of millions of billions of bees by which it is covered, might use that honey according to his desire;
so too is the outflow-free knowledge within embodied beings, which resembles that honey.
The afflictions resemble petty creatures, while the Victor is like a man skilled in slaying them. // 104 //
The afflictions are like the outer husk,
while the tathāgatagarbha is like the inner kernel.
Just as the essence within grains, when joined with the husk, does not serve for the enjoyment of people;
But those who seek food and other such things through them liberate those very things from their husks. // 105 //
Even though it exists within sentient beings, as long as it is thus defiled by the stains of the afflictions, it does not exercise the state of a Victor;
it does not perform the work of a Perfect Buddha within the three realms of existence until it is liberated from the affliction of the stains of the afflictions. (106)
Just as the essence within kangu, śāli, kodrava, barley, and vrīhi rice, though released from its husk, does not become sweet, well-prepared, or palatable food for men;

In the same way, the Lord of Dharma, whose body has not yet emerged from the husk of the afflictions, does not bestow the flavor of the joy of the Dharma upon beings who are tormented by the hunger of the afflictions. (107)
The afflictions are like a heap of impure refuse,
while the *tathāgatagarbha* is like gold.
Just as gold might fall from a man walking along into a heap of putrid refuse, so it is with this.
It would remain there in that very same state for many hundreds of years, possessing the nature of being indestructible.
The deity, having perceived this with his divine, purified eye, shall speak there to the man:
"There is gold here, a ninth and foremost jewel; having purified it, perform your task with that jewel."

Seeing that the quality of being in sentient beings was likewise submerged in afflictions—comparable to a bottomless mire—the Sage released a rain of Dharma upon all creatures for the sake of cleansing them from the mud of those afflictions. (110)
Just as a deity, seeing gold fallen into a heap of impure filth— the most beautiful thing for men— would point it out for the sake of purifying it from its stains;
even so, the Victor [points out] the Jewel of the Perfectly Awakened One fallen into the great impurity of the afflictions.
Having surveyed sentient beings, he taught the Dharma for the purification of embodied beings. // 111 //
The afflictions are like the surface of the earth,
and the tathāgata-element is like a treasure of jewels. For example, suppose there were an inexhaustible treasure within the ground inside the house of a poor man.
That man would not recognize him, nor would he say to that treasure, "I am this. // 112 //

In the same way, this world of beings, though possessing within its own mind an inconceivable, inexhaustible, and stainless treasury of jewels of virtuous qualities, yet failing to realize it, incessantly experiences the manifold suffering of poverty. (113)
Just as a treasure of jewels situated within the house of a poor man would not say to him, "I am here," nor would the man know it,
so too sentient beings are like the poor, for the treasure of the Dharma resides within their own minds.
The cause for their attainment is that a Sage arises in the world. // 114 //
The afflictions are like the husk of a seed,
while the tathāgata-element is like the seed and sprout;
just as within the fruits of trees such as the mango and the palmyra, the seed and sprout exist as something whose nature is indestructible.
Planted in the earth, through its union with water and other conditions, it gradually attains the state of a king of trees. // 115 //

The pure realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), enveloped within the inner sheath of the bark-like fruit of ignorance in sentient beings, gradually attains the state of a King of Sages by depending upon various wholesome qualities, just like that [tree]. (116)
Just as a tree arises from the interior of the shell of a palm fruit or a mango fruit through the conditions of water, the sun's rays, wind, earth, time, and space,
so too does the sprout of the seed of the Perfectly Awakened One exist within the bark of the fruit of a sentient being's afflictions.
In the same way, the tree of Dharma grows through those various auspicious conditions. // 117 //
The afflictions are like putrid rags;
the *tathāgatagarbha* is like a precious statue.
Just as a statue made of jewels belonging to the Victor might be enclosed within foul-smelling, putrid garments, so it is with this.
Having seen [the body] abandoned on the road, a deity would speak this matter to a traveler for the sake of his liberation: 118.

Just as one who possesses unimpeded vision, beholding the body of a Sugata though it be shrouded by the stains of various afflictions, applies a means for its liberation even when it is among animals, so too does he act. // 119 //
Just as one with divine vision, seeing a body of a Tathāgata made of jewels cast away on the road and covered by foul-smelling rags, might show it to people for their liberation;
even so, [the Buddha] shows that which is covered by the putrid garments of the afflictions and cast away on the path of saṃsāra.
Having surveyed the realm among the animals, the Jina taught the Dharma for the sake of liberation. // 120 //
The afflictions are like a woman who has conceived a fetus;
the tathāgata-element is like a universal monarch existing within the primary elements of the *kalala* stage.
Just as some woman, being destitute and deformed, might dwell in a house for the homeless...
Carrying royal splendor within her womb, she did not realize that the king was in her own belly.
Rebirth in existence is like a house for the destitute, and impure beings are like pregnant women;
that stainless element is like the embryo within them, for when it is present, they possess a protector. (122)
Just as a woman whose body is covered in soiled garments, possessing a loathsome appearance, experiences supreme suffering in a masterless house while a king dwells within her womb,
so too do people, their minds unpeaceful due to the power of the afflictions, abide in a dwelling place of suffering.
And they consider themselves to be without a protector, even though their protectors are present within their own selves. 123.

The afflictions are like a coating of clay, while the *tathāgatagarbha* is like a golden image. Just as one might see a golden statue filled with molten gold inside, yet appearing externally as a mere object made of clay; so too is the nature of the Tathāgata.
Just as one skilled in gold would remove external impurities for the sake of the internal purity of the gold, so too [should one act]. (124)

Constantly observing that the nature [of the mind] is luminous and that defilements are merely adventitious, the Supreme Enlightenment purifies the world—which resembles a mine of jewels—from its obscurations in this manner. (125)
Just as a skilled jeweler, perceiving that an image made of pure, radiant gold might be hidden within clay,
would remove the earth; so too does the Omniscient One, perceiving the mind to be peaceful and resembling pure gold, [remove the defilements].
By means of the method of teaching the Dharma and the application of blows, he impels one toward the removal of obscurations. // 126 //
The summarized meaning of the examples is as follows:
in a lotus, a bee, breath, husks, excrement, and the earth;
and likewise in the skin of a fruit, a foul garment, the womb of a woman, and the interior of a clay pot. (127)
Like a Buddha, like honey, like the cream of ghee, like a treasure of gold, like a tree, like a precious statue, like a universal monarch, and like a golden image. // 128 //

The stainlessness of the nature of the mind within the realm of sentient beings is declared to be beginningless, even though it is unconnected with the sheaths of afflictions that are themselves beginningless. (129)

In brief, by this exposition of the illustrations from the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, it is demonstrated that for the entire realm of sentient beings, the phenomena of the beginningless defilement of the mind are adventitious, whereas the phenomena of the beginningless purification of the mind are co-nate and inseparable.
Therefore it is said:
"Through the defilement of the mind, sentient beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind, they are purified.
In this regard, what is the defilement of the mind with reference to which the teaching of the ninefold analogies, such as the lotus calyx and so forth, is given?

The stains consisting of the latencies of intense outbursts of passion, hatred, and delusion, which reside in the stages purified by the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, [are abandoned]. // 130 //
By means of similes such as the lotus bud and others, [the tathāgatagarbha] is revealed in nine ways;
however, when distinguished by their varieties, there are infinite millions of sheaths of secondary afflictions.
In brief, these nine afflictions exist as mere adventitious stains within the naturally pure *tathāgatagarbha*, just as the sheaths of lotuses and so forth exist around the images of the Buddha.
What are the nine? They are as follows: first, the affliction characterized by the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of passion (*rāga*).
It is characterized by the latent tendency of hatred;
it is characterized by the latent tendency of delusion;
and it is characterized by the active outbursts of intense passion, hatred, and delusion.
It is comprised within the ground of the latency of ignorance;
it is to be abandoned by vision;
it is to be abandoned by cultivation.
There are those belonging to the impure stages and those belonging to the pure stages. Among them,

those afflictions existing within the mental continua of worldly beings who are free from passion— which are the causes for the accumulation of immovable formative forces (*saṃskāra*), which give rise to the realms of form and formlessness, and which are to be destroyed by supramundane knowledge— are said to be characterized by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of attachment, aversion, and delusion.
Thus:

those [afflictions] residing in the mental continua of sentient beings whose conduct is dominated by passion and so forth, which are the causes for the accumulation of meritorious and non-meritorious formative forces (*saṃskāra*), which produce solely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and which are to be destroyed by the knowledge of the meditative cultivation of the foul (*aśubha*) and so forth— these are called "characterized by the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) of intense passion, hatred, and delusion."

Those [afflictions] belonging to the continuum of Arhats which are the causes for the activity of untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*), which produce the stainless mind-made body (*vimala-manomaya-ātmabhāva*), and which are to be destroyed by the Tathāgata’s wisdom of enlightenment—these are called "comprised within the ground of the latency of ignorance" (*avidyāvāsabhūmi-saṃgṛhīta*).
There are two kinds of those in training (*śaikṣa*): the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and the noble one (*ārya*).

In this regard, those [afflictions] residing in the continuums of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*), which are to be destroyed by the knowledge that perceives the first supramundane dharma, are called "to be abandoned by seeing" (*darśana-prahātavya*). Those residing in the continuums of noble persons (*āryapudgala*) in training, which are to be destroyed by the knowledge of cultivation regarding the supramundane dharmas as they have been seen, are called "to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Those residing in the continuums of bodhisattvas who have not yet reached the final goal, which are the adversaries (*vipakṣa*) of the seven kinds of knowledge-bhūmis and are to be destroyed by the knowledge of cultivation belonging to the three bhūmis beginning with the eighth, are called "belonging to the impure stages" (*aśuddha-bhūmi-gata*).

Those [afflictions] residing in the mental continuum of bodhisattvas who have reached the culmination, which are the adversaries of the knowledge of cultivation on the three stages beginning with the eighth, and which are to be destroyed by the knowledge of the diamond-like samādhi, are called "those belonging to the pure stages.
These nine afflictions, beginning with attachment, are briefly elucidated in their respective order through nine similes, such as the sheath of a lotus and so forth. // 132 //

Furthermore, in detail, these very [qualities], through their division into eighty-four thousand types, become as infinite as the wisdom of the Tathāgata. By means of these, the *tathāgatagarbha*—hidden within the sheaths of limitless afflictions—is rendered impure for the foolish, for arhats, and for wise trainees (*śaikṣas*), respectively, by four, one, two, and two stains. (133)
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"All sentient beings are the *tathāgatagarbha*.
In this regard, "all sentient beings" are stated briefly to be of four kinds, namely: ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), arhats, those in training (*śaikṣa*), and bodhisattvas.
In that regard, within this untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), their impurity is elucidated respectively by four, one, two, and two afflictive stains (*kleśamala*).
Furthermore, how are these nine afflictions, beginning with attachment (*rāga*), to be understood as being similar to the sheaths of a lotus and so forth?
And how is the correspondence between the *tathāgatadhātu* and the images of a Buddha and so forth to be understood?
Just as that lotus, having first arisen from the mud and been beautiful to the mind, later became unpleasant; so too is the delight in passion.
Just as angry bees sting living beings most violently, so too does hatred, when it arises in the heart, produce suffering. (135)
Just as the kernel of rice and other grains is concealed on the outside by husks, so too the vision of the essential reality is concealed within the shell of the egg of delusion. (136)
Just as impurity is repulsive, so are sensual desires to those free from passion; because they are the cause for indulging in sensual desires, the outbursts of passion are like impurity. (137)
Just as people might fail to find a treasure hidden beneath the earth due to ignorance,
so too do beings remain obscured by the ground of the dwelling of ignorance regarding their own self-existent nature.

Just as the husk of a seed is destroyed through the gradual emergence of the sprout and so forth, so too is there the cessation of those things to be abandoned by vision through the realization of reality. // 139 //

For those who have destroyed the essence of the view of a self-identity through adherence to the Noble Path, there is the illustration of a rotten garment regarding those [defilements] to be abandoned by the knowledge of cultivation. (140)
The impurities residing in the seven stages are like the impurities within the womb; non-conceptual gnosis is like the matured embryo once it has emerged from the womb. (141)

The impurities associated with the three stages should be known as being like a coating of clay and mud; they are to be destroyed by the knowledge of the diamond-like samādhi of the Great Beings. 142.

Thus, the nine impurities, beginning with passion, are comparable to the lotus and so forth; the element possesses a commonality with the Buddha and others because it comprises the three natures. (143)
With reference to its threefold nature, the ninefold similarity of the *tathāgatagarbha* to the reflection of a Buddha and so forth should be understood for the sake of the purification of the mind.
What are these three natures?
Its nature is the *dharmakāya*, suchness (*tathatā*), and also the lineage (*gotra*).
He is to be known through three, one, and five illustrations. // 144 //

That element, which has the *dharmakāya* as its intrinsic nature, is to be understood through three analogies—the Buddha’s image, honey, and the kernel of grain; that which has *tathatā* as its intrinsic nature, through one analogy—gold;

and that which has the lineage (*gotra*) as its intrinsic nature for the arising of the three types of Buddha-bodies, through five analogies—a treasure, a tree, a precious statue, a universal monarch, and a golden image.
In that regard, what is the Dharma-body?
The Dharma-body is to be known as twofold: the utterly stainless realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and its natural outflow, which is the teaching of the methods of profundity and diversity. // 145 //
The *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas is to be understood as twofold:
first, the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*, which is the objective domain of non-conceptual gnosis;
and this is to be known with reference to the dharma realized within oneself by the Tathāgatas.

And the cause for attaining that [state] is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*, which arises as communication (*vijñapti*) toward other beings according to their needs for discipline (*vainayika*).
This should be understood with reference to the Dharma of teaching (*deśanādharma*).
Furthermore, teaching is of two kinds, due to the distinction in the methods of establishing the subtle and the gross Dharma.

Namely: the teaching of the method for establishing the profound Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka with reference to ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); and the teaching of the method for establishing various Dharmas—such as the diverse sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, and so forth—with reference to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Because it is supramundane, no worldly analogies for it can be found.
The Tathāgata himself has established the similarity between [the Buddha] and the element (dhātu). // 146 //
The teaching of the subtle and profound method should be known as being like honey of a single flavor;
the teaching of various methods should be known as being like the diverse essences within eggs. // 147 //

Thus, by means of these three similes—the Buddha-image, honey, and the kernel—it has been elucidated that all sentient beings are the embryos of the Tathāgata, with reference to the fact that the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata pervades the entire realm of sentient beings without exception. Indeed, there is no being whatsoever to be found in the realm of sentient beings who exists outside the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, just as form does not exist outside the realm of space. For it is said:
Just as space is always considered omnipresent, so too is that [Tathāgata-garbha] always considered omnipresent;
just as space is all-pervading among all forms, so too is it all-pervading among the multitudes of sentient beings.
Because its nature is unchanging, auspicious, and pure, the simile of a gold disk is cited with respect to suchness. (148)

That mind, although accompanied by phenomena of infinite afflictions and suffering, is called *tathatā* (suchness) in the sense of being unchanging, like fine gold, because it is naturally luminous and thus not subject to transformation;

and when that [mind], which is essentially indistinguishable in all sentient beings—even those whose mental continuums are fixed in falsehood—has attained purification from all adventitious defilements, it receives the designation "Tathāgata."

Thus, by means of this single analogy of gold, with reference to the meaning of the non-differentiation from suchness (*tathatā*), it has been elucidated that "the Tathāgata is the *tathatā*-womb (*garbha*) of all these sentient beings," based upon the non-dual nature of the purity of the mind's intrinsic nature (*cittaprakṛtiviśuddhyadvayadharmatā*), as stated by the Blessed One:
"In this regard, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is one who has thoroughly understood the root of the appropriation of a self."
Through the purity of the self, one conforms to the purity of all sentient beings.

That which is the purity of the self and that which is the purity of sentient beings—this is non-dual and without distinction. Thus it is said: "Although suchness is undifferentiated for all, it has attained purity."
Therefore, the state of a Tathāgata exists, and all embodied beings possess that embryo.
That lineage should be known as twofold, like a treasure and a fruit-bearing tree:
that which abides in its primordial nature from beginningless time, and that which is further developed through cultivation. (149)
The attainment of the three bodies of a Buddha is considered to result from these two lineages:
from the first comes the first body, and from the second come the latter two. (150)
The pure essential body (svābhāvikakāya) should be known as being like a jewel-image, because it is unconditioned by nature and because it is the locus for the jewels of its qualities. // 151 //
Because it is the great sovereign king of the Dharma, the Enjoyment Body is like a universal monarch;
because its nature is that of a reflection, the Emanation Body is like a golden image. // 152 //
Thus, by means of these remaining five similes— the treasure, the tree, the precious image, the universal monarch, and the golden statue—

with reference to the meaning of the nature of the lineage (*gotra*) from which the threefold body of the Buddha arises, it has been demonstrated that "the *tathāgatadhātu* is the embryo (*garbha*) within all sentient beings.
For the state of a *Tathāgata* is indeed characterized by the manifestation of the threefold body of the Buddha.
Therefore, the *tathāgatadhātu* is the cause for its attainment; here, the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*) is the meaning of "cause. For it is said:
And therein, within every single sentient being, the *tathāgata*-element has arisen and exists as an embryo (*garbha*), yet those sentient beings do not realize it. For thus it is said:
"The element is beginningless and the common support of all phenomena; because it exists, there are all states of existence as well as the attainment of *nirvāṇa*."
In that regard, how is it beginningless?
It is because, with reference specifically to the *tathāgatagarbha*, the Blessed One taught and designated that "no prior limit is discerned," referring to it as the "element" (*dhātu*).
As it is said:
"O Blessed One, that which is this *tathāgatagarbha*, the supramundane embryo, the naturally pure embryo."
Regarding "the common basis of all phenomena":

as it is said, "Therefore, Blessed One, the *tathāgatagarbha* is the support, the foundation, and the ground of the unconditioned phenomena that are connected, inseparable, and not released from gnosis."

O Blessed One, the *tathāgatagarbha* is the support, the foundation, and the basis for all conditioned phenomena—even those that are unconnected, characterized by separability, and devoid of knowledge.
Because it exists, there is "going" (transmigration) for all;
as it has been said:
O Blessed One, since the Tathāgatagarbha exists, the conceptualization that there is "saṃsāra" is merely a verbal designation;
likewise, the attainment of "nirvāṇa" is also [merely a designation].
As it has been said:

"Blessed One, if the *tathāgatagarbha* did not exist, there would be no weariness with suffering, nor would there be the desire, longing, aspiration, or vow for *nirvāṇa*," and so forth in detail. Indeed, this *tathāgatagarbha*— which is non-separate from the *dharmakāya*, characterized by its indivisibility from *tathatā*, and having the nature of a determined lineage (*niyatagotra*)—
should be understood as existing at all times and in all places throughout the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) in its entirety, taking the *dharmatā* as the authoritative standard.
As it has been said:
"O son of good family, this is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā):
whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, these sentient beings are always possessed of the tathāgatagarbha."
And that very *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is itself here the reasoning, the yoga, the means, and the synonym;
it must be exactly so,
and otherwise it could not be so.
In all cases, the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) alone is the refuge;
the very nature of phenomena alone is the reasoning for the settling of the mind and the realization of the mind.
That [nature] is not to be thought about, nor is it to be conceptualized, but is to be resolved upon with conviction (*adhimoktavya*).
