The ultimate truth of the Self-Existent Ones must be followed through faith alone; for one without eyes cannot behold the blazing orb of the sun. (153)
In brief, these four types of persons are established as being without the eye to see the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Which four?
Namely: the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the disciple (*śrāvaka*), the solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*), and the bodhisattva who has newly set out in the vehicle (*navayāna-saṃprasthita*).
As it has been said:

"O Blessed One, this *tathāgatagarbha* is not the domain of those who have fallen into the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), those who delight in perversions (*viparyāsa*), or those whose minds are distracted by emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
In this context, those who have fallen into the view of a self-identity are called ordinary worldlings (*bālapṛthagjana*).

For they, having accepted those phenomena such as the aggregates—which are utterly subject to outflows—as "self" and "belonging to self," are so deeply attached to the notions of "I" and "mine" that they are not even capable of resolving upon the realm free from outflows, which is the cessation of the view of a real body;
how much less could they realize the Tathāgatagarbha, the object of the Omniscient One?
This is impossible.
In this context, those who delight in perversion are said to be the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Why is that?

For even they, while the Tathāgatagarbha—which is eternal—is to be cultivated as something superior, instead of cultivating the perception of its eternity, they delight in cultivating the perception of impermanence through their perversion.

While the *tathāgatagarbha* is blissful and should be further cultivated as such, they delight in cultivating the perception of suffering through the perversion of cultivating the perception of bliss regarding it.

While the *tathāgatagarbha* is the self and should be further cultivated as such, they delight in cultivating the perception of non-self through the perversion of cultivating the perception of self regarding it.

While the *tathāgatagarbha* is pure and should be further cultivated as such, they delight in cultivating the perception of impurity through the perversion of cultivating the perception of purity regarding it.

Thus, by this method, it is said that this element—characterized by supreme permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity—is not the domain even of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, because they delight in paths that are devoid of the attainment of the Dharmakāya.

And just as it is not the domain of those who delight in revulsion and perceive things as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure, so too has the Blessed One explained at length in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* by means of the analogy of the jewel in the water of a pond.

Monks, it is just as if, during the summer season, people were playing in the water after building a dam and adorning themselves with their various ornaments and enjoyments. Then, suppose one person were to place a genuine lapis lazuli gem beneath the water.
Consequently, for the sake of that lapis lazuli, they would all cast off their ornaments and dive in.

Then, whatever gravel or pebbles were there, thinking "this is a jewel," they would pick them up; and repeatedly exclaiming, "I have found a jewel," they would stand on the bank of the pond and form the perception that "this is not a jewel.
And yet, by the power of the jewel, that water of the pond would continue to shine with its radiance.
Thus, seeing that water shining in such a way, the perception of its qualities would arise in them, thinking, "Aha! It is a jewel!
Then, one among them who was skillful in means and wise would obtain the jewel in its true nature.
In the very same way, monks, you [should understand] that everything is impermanent, everything is suffering, everything is non-self, and everything is impure.

"By the inclusion of the word 'all,' [it is meant that] all those things—whether cultivated or repeatedly cultivated—which are fashioned by those who do not know the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*), are useless.
Therefore, monks, do not be like those standing in a pond full of pebbles and gravel; rather, you must become skilled in means (*upāyakuśala*)."

Monks, whatever you have cultivated and repeatedly practiced by means of the universal application that "everything is impermanent, everything is suffering, everything is non-self, and everything is impure," and yet [perceive] therein permanence, pleasure, purity, and self— this detailed exposition on the establishment of the supreme reality of dharmas, which is the instruction on the nature of perversion, is to be understood in detail according to the Sūtra.

In this regard, those whose minds are distracted by emptiness are said to be bodhisattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle and have lost their way regarding the method of the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*-emptiness.

They desire the door of liberation that is emptiness for the sake of destroying existing entities, thinking that the subsequent cessation and destruction of an entity that truly exists is *parinirvāṇa*.
Or again, they resort to emptiness through the apprehension of emptiness, thinking: "Emptiness is some entity distinct from form and so forth, which we shall realize and cultivate."
In this regard, what is called the principle of the meaning of the emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha*?
(Rgv 76) Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added. Reality is to be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated. // 154 //
The realm is empty of adventitious factors characterized by separability, but it is not empty of the unsurpassed dharmas characterized by inseparability. (155)
What is illuminated by this?
Since there is nothing to be removed from this naturally pure *tathāgata*-element— because its nature is emptiness of adventitious stains that serve as the cause of defilement—
and since there is nothing to be added to it as a cause of purification— because its nature consists of inseparable pure qualities.
Therefore it is said:
"The *tathāgatagarbha* is empty of all the sheaths of afflictions (*kleśa-kośa*), which are separable and characterized by being abandoned through knowledge;

yet it is not empty of the inconceivable Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*), which exceed the sands of the river Ganges, are inseparable, and are characterized by not being abandoned through knowledge."
Thus, one correctly perceives that whatever is not present in a certain place is empty of that;
furthermore, one understands as it truly is that whatever remains there exists here as a reality.
By thus avoiding the extremes of superimposition and denial, the limitless characteristic of emptiness is elucidated by these two verses.

In this regard, those whose minds wander away from this method of the meaning of emptiness, dispersing and not becoming concentrated or one-pointed, are said to have minds distracted by emptiness (*śūnyatā-vikṣiptacitta*).
Indeed, without the gateway of the knowledge of ultimate emptiness, it is impossible to realize or directly perceive the non-conceptual realm (*nirvikalpa-dhātu*).
And it was with this in mind that it was said:
The very gnosis of the *tathāgatagarbha* is the gnosis of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) for the Tathāgatas;
and this *tathāgatagarbha* has never before been seen or realized by any of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—such is the detailed explanation.

Indeed, this *tathāgatagarbha*, insofar as it is the womb of the *dharmadhātu*, is said to be beyond the range of those fallen into the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because the *dharmadhātu* is the antidote to such views.

Just as the *dharmakāya*—the womb (*garbha*) of supramundane phenomena—is said to be beyond the range of those who delight in perversions, because it reveals supramundane phenomena as the antidote to mundane phenomena such as impermanence;

so too, the womb of phenomena that are naturally pure is said to be beyond the range of those distracted by emptiness, because the qualities of purity—which are manifested by the supramundane *dharmakāya* and are inseparable from it—are by nature empty of adventitious stains.

In this regard, that which is intended here as the vision of knowledge according to reality (*yathābhūtajñānadarśana*) is the contemplation of the natural purity of the supramundane *dharmakāya*, having relied upon the gateway of the knowledge of the non-differentiation of the single-principle *dharmadhātu*. It is by means of this that it is said that Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages see the *tathāgatagarbha* slightly. For thus it is said:
"Like the sun in a sky with gaps in the clouds, you are seen here by those with the pure eye of awakening."
Even by the Noble Ones, you are not perceived in your entirety by their limited intellects; however,
O Blessed One, those whose wisdom is infinite behold your Dharma-body in its totality as it extends through the infinite expanse of the sky of the knowable.

If this realm is thus difficult to perceive even for the supreme noble ones who are established on the stage of ultimate non-attachment, then what is the purpose of teaching it by starting with ordinary foolish worldlings?
There are two verses summarizing the purpose of this teaching: [The verses follow.]
With the first [verse] there is the question, and with the second, the explanation:
"Everything is empty in every way; in this and that [context], the knowable is like clouds, dreams, and magical illusions.
Having said this, why has it been stated here by the Buddhas that the Buddha-element exists in every sentient being? // 156 //

A sunken mind, contempt for inferior beings, grasping at the unreal, denial of real dharmas, and excessive self-attachment—these are the five faults; it was taught for the sake of their abandonment. // 157 //
The meaning of these two verses should indeed be understood in brief through ten verses:
"All conditioned phenomena in every respect are, within the limits of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), devoid [of intrinsic nature];
they are illustrated by examples such as clouds and so forth, in the sense that they are [the results of] afflictions, karma, and maturation. (158)
The afflictions are like clouds; their functional activity is like the enjoyment of a dream;
and the aggregates, which are the maturation of afflictions and karma, are like magical illusions. (159)
Having established it thus previously, here again in this later tantra, the existence of the element (dhātu) is revealed for the sake of abandoning the five faults. (160)
For indeed, because they have not heard this, the mind directed toward enlightenment does not arise in certain individuals of inferior disposition due to the fault of self-contempt. (161)
Even when the thought of awakening has arisen in him, one who thinks "I am superior" develops the notion of inferiority toward those whose minds have not yet produced the thought of awakening. (162)
For one who holds such a view, right knowledge does not arise; consequently, they grasp at what is unreal and fail to perceive the real truth. (163)
Those faults of sentient beings are unreal, because they are artificial and adventitious;
their lack of self (nairātmya) regarding those faults is real, for the qualities are pure by nature.
Grasping at non-existent faults and disparaging real virtues, the wise one does not attain loving-kindness that perceives the equality of beings and self. (165)
From hearing that, there arises for him enthusiasm, reverence for the Teacher, wisdom, knowledge, and great loving-kindness; thus, five qualities emerge from that. (166)
Free from contempt, viewing all equally, faultless, and possessed of virtues, he who has equal affection for himself and for all beings swiftly attains Buddhahood. (167)

Thus ends the first chapter, the Section on the Tathāgatagarbha, in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, the Treatise on the Ultimate Continuum of the Mahāyāna, by way of an explanatory summary of the meaning of the verses. // 1 //
2. Second Chapter:
Thusness with Impurity has been explained.
Now, stainless suchness (*nirmalā tathatā*) must be explained.

In that regard, what is stainless suchness? It is that which, in the uncontaminated realm (*anāsravadhātu*) of the Blessed Buddhas, is established as the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) due to the departure of all forms of defilement.
Furthermore, it should be understood briefly with reference to eight topics.

What are the eight topics? They are: purity, attainment, dissociation, the welfare of oneself and others, their basis, profundity, vastness, and magnanimity; as well as for how long and in what manner these exist. (1)
Thus, these eight categories are elucidated by this verse in their respective order:

namely, the meaning of intrinsic nature, the meaning of cause, the meaning of fruit, the meaning of activity, the meaning of union, the meaning of manifestation, the meaning of permanence, and the meaning of inconceivability.
In this regard, that which is called the *tathāgatagarbha* by the Blessed One is the element (*dhātu*) that is not yet freed from the sheath of afflictions.
The purification of that [tathāgatagarbha] should be understood as having the nature of the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*),
because it is said:

"O Blessed One, whoever is free from doubt regarding the tathāgatagarbha hidden within the millions of sheaths of all afflictions is also free from doubt regarding the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata, which is liberated from the sheaths of all afflictions."
Knowledge is twofold: supramundane non-conceptual [knowledge] and that which is subsequently attained.
Mundane and supramundane knowledge is the cause for the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), and it is elucidated by the term "attainment" (*prāpti*).
It is called "attainment" because one attains [the goal] by means of it.
That fruit is twofold.
Disjunction is twofold: disjunction from the obscuration of afflictions and disjunction from the obscuration of the knowable.
Their function is, respectively, the accomplishment of one's own welfare and the welfare of others.
Yoga is the possession of that basis.

It is the constant activity, until the end of existence, in an inconceivable manner through the three Buddha-bodies manifested by profundity, magnificence, and majesty; this is "vṛtti" (activity). The summary verse:
[It is explained] by way of essence, cause, and fruit; and by way of activity, yoga, and manifestation.
And because of that very permanence and inconceivability, there is abiding upon the stages of a Buddha. // 2 //
In this regard, concerning the meaning of its intrinsic nature and the meaning of its cause, there is a verse on Buddhahood and the means for attaining it:
Buddhahood is said to be luminous by nature, like the sun and the sky when veiled by a dense mass of clouds consisting of adventitious afflictions and the thick net of the knowable.
It is endowed with all the stainless qualities of a Buddha, and is eternal, stable, and everlasting.
It is attained by relying upon the knowledge that discerns phenomena without conceptual construction. // 3 //
The meaning of this verse is to be understood in brief through the following four verses:
"Buddhahood is characterized by inseparable pure qualities; like the sun and the sky, it is defined by the two aspects of gnosis and abandonment. (4)
It is endowed with all the luminous Buddha-qualities, which exceed the sands of the Ganges in number, are unconditioned, and exist in an inseparable manner. // 5 //

Because they are unestablished by way of intrinsic nature, because they are all-pervasive, and because they are adventitious, the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable are therefore said to be like clouds. (6)
Furthermore, the cause for the separation from the two obscurations is the twofold gnosis;
that gnosis is held to be both non-conceptual and that which is subsequently attained. (7)
Regarding what was stated—that the nature of the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) is purity—therein, purity is briefly of two kinds:
natural purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and purity from stain (*vaimalya-viśuddhi*).
Among these, natural purity is that liberation which is not a dissociation (*visaṃyoga*), because the luminous nature of the mind is not dissociated from adventitious stains.

Purity as stainlessness (*vaimalya-viśuddhi*) is liberation (*vimukti*) and dissociation (*visaṃyoga*), because the luminous nature of the mind (*citta-prakṛti*) is dissociated from adventitious stains without remainder, just as water and other substances are [separated] from dust, mud, and so forth.
Regarding that purity as stainlessness, there are two verses concerning the meaning of the fruit:
Like a lake of pure water, rich with rows of blooming lotuses...
The entire moon, once released from the mouth of Rāhu,
shines like the sun whose rays are freed from the affliction of clouds and the like;
because it is endowed with stainless qualities, that very [moon] appears liberated.
Victory over the state of being a Conqueror (jina) is like a bull among sages, the essence of honey, gold, jewels, a preeminent treasure, and a tree bearing great fruit;
it is the Sugata’s stainless jewel-body, the supreme sovereign, and a golden image. 9.
The meaning of these two verses should be understood in brief through the following eight verses:
"The purification of adventitious afflictions such as passion and so forth, like [the clearing of] a lake and so on—this is stated in brief as the fruit of non-conceptual gnosis. (10)
The manifestation of the state of a Buddha endowed with the excellence of all modes is explained as the fruit of the subsequently attained gnosis. // 11 //

Because it removes the turbidity of the dust of passion like a clear lake of water, and because it causes the water of meditation to flow for the sake of those to be trained who are like lotuses, that [teaching] is so called. // 12 //
Because it is liberated from the Rāhu of hatred by means of the rays of great loving-kindness and compassion, and because it pervades the world, it is like the full, stainless moon. (13)
Through the release from the cloud-net of delusion, by dispelling darkness in the world with the rays of knowledge, that Buddhahood is like the stainless sun. (14)

Because it possesses both incomparable and comparable qualities, because it bestows the flavor of the true Dharma, and because it has removed all that is worthless, it is like the essence of honey from a Sugata. (15)
Because it is pure, because it eliminates the poverty of qualities and material wealth, and because it bestows the fruit of liberation, it is like gold, a treasure-trove, and a tree. // 16 //
Because it has the nature of the jewel of the Dharma, because it is the sovereignty over the foremost of bipeds, and because it has the form of a jewel, it is like a precious king’s image. // 17 //

As for that twofold knowledge—the supramundane non-conceptual [knowledge] and the subsequently attained knowledge—it is the cause of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) which is designated as the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*).
Its activity is said to be the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others.
In this regard, what is the perfection of the welfare of oneself and others?

The attainment of the unobstructed *dharmakāya* through liberation from the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obscurations to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*) is called the fulfillment of one's own welfare (*svārthasaṃpatti*). The subsequent spontaneous manifestation, up to the limits of the world, of the two types of mastery—namely, appearing in the two bodies and teaching—is called the fulfillment of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpatti*).
Regarding that fulfillment of the welfare of oneself and others, there are three verses concerning its activity (*karman*).

The state of a Tathāgata is untainted, all-pervading, and characterized by indestructibility; it is the firm, auspicious, eternal, and infallible ground. Like the sky, it is the cause for the experience of the objects of the six sense-faculties for the wise. (18)

It is always the sign for perceiving the meaning of the forms of the Buddha’s manifestations; it is the pure hearing of excellent teachings; likewise, it is the smelling of the pure morality of the Tathāgatas, and the finding of a drop of the supreme essence of the noble and true Dharma. (19)

In the experience of the bliss of the touch of meditative concentration, and in the awakening to the principle of the profound intrinsic nature—[the Tathāgata is] the sky of the Tathāgata, which is the abode of the ultimate truth of subtle reflection and is free from all signs. // 20 //
The meaning of these three verses should indeed be understood in brief through the following eight verses:
"In brief, this activity of the two types of gnosis should be known as the fulfillment of the liberation-body and the purification of the dharma-body. (21)
The liberation-body and the dharma-body should be understood as being twofold and yet onefold, because they are untainted, all-pervading, and constitute the unconditioned state. // 22 //
The state of being untainted (*anāsravatva*) results from the cessation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their latent impressions (*savāsanā*);
the pervasiveness (*vyāpitā*) of gnosis is considered to arise from its being unattached and unimpeded. (23)

The state of being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtatva*) consists in the essential nature of absolute non-destruction; non-destructibility is the brief statement (*uddeśa*), while its detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*) is given by means of terms such as "constant" (*dhruva*).
Destruction is to be known as fourfold, being the opposite of permanence and the other [qualities]: fulfillment, transformation, annihilation, and the inconceivable fall from one's station. // 25 //
Due to the absence of that [obscuration], it should be known as certain, auspicious, eternal, and infallible; that state is stainless knowledge because it is the locus of pure qualities. // 26 //
Just as space is the cause for the perception of form, so too is it the cause for the hearing and other [sensory perceptions] of sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena. (27)
For the wise, the two bodies are likewise the cause for the arising of untainted qualities regarding the objects of the senses, by virtue of being endowed with non-obstruction. (28)
When it was said that "the Buddha has the characteristic of space," that was spoken with reference to the ultimate, unique characteristic of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
For thus he said: "If the Tathāgata were to be seen by means of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, then even a universal monarch (cakravartin) would be a Tathāgata."
Regarding that, there is a verse concerning the meaning of "yoga" with respect to the characteristic of the ultimate truth:
It is inconceivable, eternal, stable, auspicious, and everlasting; it is quiescent, all-pervading, free from conceptual construction, and like space.
Unattached everywhere, unimpeded, free from harsh touch, invisible, ungraspable, and pure—such is the stainless state of Buddhahood. // 29 //
Now, indeed, the meaning of this verse should be understood in brief through eight verses:
The welfare of oneself and others is demonstrated by means of the liberation-body (*vimuktikāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Upon that basis of the welfare of oneself and others, there is application through qualities such as inconceivability and so forth. (30)

Buddhahood, which is the object of the knowledge of the Omniscient One, must be understood as inconceivable by those whose bodies are wisdom, because it is not within the scope of the three types of cognition. (31)

It is not an object of hearing because of its subtlety; it is not an object of reflection from the perspective of ultimate reality; and it is not an object of mundane or other forms of cultivation because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is profound. // 32 //

For that has never been seen before by the foolish, like a mass of darkness to those blind from birth; nor has it been seen by the noble ones, like the orb of the newborn sun to one staying within a maternity chamber. (33)
It is eternal because it is free from arising; it is steadfast because it is free from cessation;
it is auspicious because it is devoid of duality; and it is permanent because it abides in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). // 34 //

It is quiescent because it is the truth of cessation; it is all-pervasive because of its universal awakening; it is non-conceptual because it is non-abiding; and it is unattached because of the abandonment of the afflictions. // 35 //
It is unimpeded everywhere due to the purification of all cognitive obscurations;
it is free from harsh touch because of its softness and adaptability. // 36 //
It is invisible because it is formless; it is ungraspable because it is signless;
it is pure because it is pure by nature; and it is stainless because of the removal of defilements. // 37 //

Furthermore, it should be understood that although the state of a Tathāgata exists as inseparable from the qualities of the unconditioned— like space— it nevertheless proceeds effortlessly, without interruption or cessation, throughout the course of existence for the sake of establishing the welfare and happiness of the world, by means of the three stainless bodies— the svābhāvika, sāmbhogika, and nairmāṇika— through the specific cultivation of inconceivable great skillful means, compassion, and wisdom; for it is endowed with the unique qualities.
In that regard, concerning the purpose of the [Buddha’s] activity, there are four verses on the classification of the Buddha-bodies:

Yogins who are concentrated and diligent behold that which has the nature of the *dharmadhātu*: it is without beginning, middle, or end; undivided; non-dual; liberated in three ways; stainless; and free from conceptual construction. (38)

Endowed with inconceivable and incomparable qualities that exceed the sands of the immeasurable Gaṅgā rivers, that stainless element of the Tathāgatas has uprooted all defects along with their latent predispositions. (39)
With a body composed of the rays of the diverse true Dharma, he exerts effort for the sake of the liberation of the world;
in his activities, he possesses a manifold nature like the king of wish-fulfilling jewels, yet he does not possess that as his intrinsic nature.

Whatever is the cause for entering the path of peace, for ripening [beings], and for granting prophecy within the worlds—that image is also always contained herein, just as the realm of form is contained within the realm of space. // 41 //
The summarized meaning of these four verses should be understood through twenty verses: That which is called "Buddhahood" is the omniscience of the Self-Arisen Ones;
it is supreme cessation, the attainment of the inconceivable, and that which is personally realized within oneself. (42)
Its differentiation consists of the three bodies, beginning with the essential body (svābhāvika-kāya), which function through qualities characterized by profundity, magnificence, and greatness. (43)
In that regard, the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) of the Buddhas should be understood, in brief, as having five characteristics and being endowed with five kinds of qualities. (44)
Unconditioned and undifferentiated, it is free from the two extremes;
it has emerged from the three obscurations of afflictions, the knowable, and the meditative attainments. // 45 //
Because it is stainless, non-conceptual, and the sphere of experience for yogins, it is luminous and pure by the very nature of the dharmadhātu. // 46 //
The essential body is endowed with immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, and incomparable qualities that have reached the perfection of purity. (47)

Because of its magnificence, because it is incalculable, because it is beyond the scope of logic, and because of its absolute isolation through the eradication of latent impressions, [the qualities] such as being immeasurable follow in sequence. (48)

Because it manifests as the Dharma-body that enjoys the various teachings, and because it never ceases its activity for the sake of sentient beings as the natural outflow of purified compassion. // 49 //

The establishment of the Enjoyment Body (sāmbhogika-kāya) is non-conceptual and effortless, fulfilling intentions exactly as they arise through the miraculous power of the wish-fulfilling gem. // 50 //
In teaching, in showing, in the non-laxity of duties, in the absence of volitional effort, and in not describing that which lacks such an intrinsic nature—diversity is said to be fivefold. (51)
Just as a gem does not possess the diversity of the conditions for its appearance,
so too the All-pervading Lord does not possess the diversity of the conditions for the existence of beings.
Having surveyed the entire world with great compassion, the Knower of the World [emanates] from his Dharmakāya a multitude of emanations in diverse forms. (53)
The Jātaka tales and his rebirth among the Tuṣita gods, his passing from there, his descent into the womb, his birth, and his skill in the various arts and crafts. (54)
The dalliance and play in the inner apartments, the renunciation, the practice of austerities, the approach to the seat of enlightenment, and the crushing of Māra’s army. (55)
He displays perfect enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the act of attaining nirvana throughout impure fields, as long as existence persists.

The Knower of Means, having caused sentient beings to feel revulsion for the three realms of existence by means of the words "impermanence," "suffering," "selflessness," and "peace," leads them across to nirvana. (57)

And those who have entered the path of peace, perceiving it as having attained nirvāṇa, [are led further] by the elucidation of the reality of the Dharma through such works as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. (58)
Having turned them away from their former attachments through the embrace of wisdom and skillful means,
he brings them to maturity in the supreme vehicle and grants them the prophecy of supreme enlightenment.
Their subtlety, the perfection of their power, and their ability to carry across even a caravan of fools—through these, one should understand their depth, loftiness, and greatness respectively. (60)
Here, the first is the Dharma-body, while the latter two are the Form-bodies;
just as a form exists within space, the last exists within the first.
Regarding the eternal nature of that very threefold body in its activity of bestowing welfare and happiness upon the world, there is this verse:

Because the causes are infinite, because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, because of the union with compassion, wisdom, and the perfection of knowledge, because of mastery over the Dharma, because of the destruction of the Māra of death, and because of the absence of self-nature, the Lord of the World is eternal. (62)

The summary meaning of this [verse] should be understood through six verses: "By the renunciation of body, life, and enjoyments; by the gathering of the true Dharma; and by fulfilling the initial vow for the benefit of all sentient beings. (63)
Because of the manifestation of perfectly pure compassion within Buddhahood,
and because of the power of their abiding through the illumination of the bases of miraculous power (ṛddhipāda), // 64 //
Through wisdom, one is liberated from the dualistic grasping at both cyclic existence and nirvana;
through this, one is endowed with the attainment of the bliss of constant, inconceivable meditative absorption. // 65 //
As he wanders through the world, he remains untainted by worldly dharmas; having attained the state of the nectar of peace, the Māra of death has no power over him. // 66 //
Because the Sage, whose nature is unconditioned, is primordially quiescent, and because he provides refuge to those who are eternally without refuge. // 67 //
The permanence of the Teacher’s form-body (rūpakāya) is established by the first seven reasons; the permanence of his dharma-body (dharmakāya) is established by the final three. (68)
And this method of attainment of the Tathāgatas, which is manifested through the revolution of the basis (āśrayaparivṛtti), is to be understood by way of the inconceivable method.
Regarding the meaning of the inconceivable, there is this verse:
Because it is inexpressible, because it comprises the ultimate truth, because it is beyond the realm of logic, and because it transcends all similes;
Because it is unsurpassed and because it does not grasp at either existence or quiescence, the domain of the Buddhas is inconceivable even for the Noble Ones. // 69 //
The summary meaning of this [verse] should be understood through four verses:

"It is inconceivable because it is ineffable; it is ineffable from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Ultimate reality is beyond the reach of thought because it cannot be inferred through reasoning. (70)

It is to be inferred through its being unsurpassed; its unsurpassedness is due to non-apprehension; non-apprehension is due to non-abiding; and non-abiding is due to the absence of conceptualization regarding qualities and defects. // 71 //
By five causes, it is inconceivable from the perspective of the *dharmakāya* due to its subtlety and so forth;
by the sixth, it is inconceivable from the perspective of the *rūpakāya* because it is not cultivated as a reality. (72)
The Victors, having reached the further shore of qualities, are inconceivable due to their qualities such as unsurpassed gnosis and great compassion;
therefore, even the Great Sages who have obtained empowerment do not understand this final stage of the Self-Existent One. // 73 //
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Chapter on Enlightenment," in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, the Great Treatise on the Ultimate Continuum of the Mahāyāna. // 2 //
3. The third chapter:
Immaculate suchness has been explained.
Those qualities which depend upon that [Buddha-nature], which—like the color and shape of the luster of a jewel—are of an undifferentiated nature and are internally stainless, must now be explained.
Immediately following this, a verse begins the classification of the Buddha’s qualities:
"One's own welfare, the welfare of others, the body of ultimate reality, and the conventional body dependent upon it."
The fruit, due to its nature as both disjunction and maturation, consists of these sixty-four distinct qualities. // 1 //
What is meant by this?
The body that is the basis for one's own perfection is the ultimate [body]; the form of the Sage that is the basis for the perfection of others is the conventional [body]. (2)

The first body is endowed with the qualities of dissociation, such as the powers and so forth; the second, however, is endowed with the marks of a Great Being that result from karmic maturation. // 3 //
From this point onward, there is a section of the text concerning suchness (*tathatā*) regarding how the powers (*bala*) and other qualities are to be understood.
The state of being a power is like a thunderbolt against the veils of ignorance; fearlessness in assemblies is like a lion;
the uniqueness of the Tathāgata is like the sky; and the twofold manifestation of the Sage is like the moon in the water. (Verse 4)
"Endowed with power" means:
regarding what is possible and impossible, the ripening of karmas, the faculties, the elements, inclinations, and the all-pervading path. (5)
Regarding the purification of the afflictions of meditation and so forth, the recollection of past abodes, the divine eye, and tranquility, there is tenfold knowledge which constitutes power. (6)
"Like a vajra" refers to:

[knowledge of] what is possible and impossible, the realms of karmic maturation, the various dispositions of the world, liberation, the method, affliction and purification, the collection of faculties, and the recollection of former abodes.

And in the divine eye and in the method for the destruction of the outflows, his power is like a thunderbolt, because it shatters, scatters, and cuts through the mountain-fortress and the trees of the armor of ignorance. // 7 //
Regarding "having attained the four grounds of self-confidence":

there are four kinds of self-confidence—regarding the perfect awakening to all phenomena, regarding the prevention of obstacles, regarding the proclamation of the path, and regarding the attainment of cessation. (8)
Because of knowing the object to be known in every respect for oneself and others; because of making known [that object] by oneself;
because of effecting the abandonment of the object to be abandoned through the cause of its abandonment; because of practicing the method to be practiced;
and because of attaining what is to be attained—the unsurpassed and exceedingly pure state—and causing others to attain it.
The noble ones possess unshakeable confidence because they speak the truth regarding the welfare of both themselves and others in certain instances. // 9 //
"Like a lion":

Just as the king of beasts is always in the depths of the forest, fearless, with an unshakable gait toward other animals; so too is the lion-like Lord of Munis among his assemblies—self-abiding, free from longing, and established in steadfast valor. (10)
"Endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha":
there is no faltering or shouting on the part of the Teacher; his mindfulness is never lost; his mind is never uncomposed; nor does he have any perception of diversity. (11)
There is no loss through equanimity or discernment, nor through desire or vigor;
[there is no loss] through mindfulness, wisdom, liberation, or the knowledge and vision of liberation. (12)
Action preceded by knowledge, and unobstructed knowledge of the three times—these eighteen and other qualities are the unique attributes of the Teacher. (13)
There is no stumbling, no noise, no loss of mindfulness in the mind, no confusion of perception, and no indifference toward his own natural state; nor is there any decline in the Sage’s zeal,
vigor, mindfulness, or his pure, stainless wisdom and liberation.
And because liberation consists in the manifestation of knowledge, through which all objects of knowledge are clearly perceived. // 14 //
The three activities regarding objects that follow immediately after all-knowledge are the constant engagement of vast, unimpeded wisdom throughout the three times;
such is this state of Buddhahood, realized by the Victors through its union with great compassion.
Through the awakening to which the great wheel of the true Dharma, the bestower of fearlessness, was set in motion in the world. // 15 //
"Like space":

that which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) in earth and the other elements is not the true nature found in space; and those qualities characterized by non-obstruction and so forth that belong to the sky do not exist in material things.
Like earth, water, fire, wind, and space, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are common throughout the worlds; yet they are never again common even within the worlds.
"Endowed with the form possessing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man":
[these are] well-placed feet marked with wheels, long and broad heels, long fingers, and hands and feet joined by a web. (17)
The skin is soft and beautiful, youthful; the body has seven protuberances; the shanks are like those of an antelope; and the private organ is concealed in a sheath like that of an elephant. (18)
The upper half of his body is like that of a lion; his shoulders are closely set; his shoulders are well-rounded; and his arms are rounded, smooth, and not protruding. (19)
(95) His arms are long and hanging down; his body is encircled by a pure halo of light;
his neck is stainless like a conch shell; and his jaw is like that of the king of beasts, symmetrical and even. 20.
He has forty teeth; his teeth are clear and without gaps; his teeth are pure and even; and his canine teeth are white and excellent. // 21 //
The self-existent one possesses a broad tongue, an endless and inconceivable excellence of taste, the warbling of a kalaviṅka bird, and a voice like that of Brahmā. // 22 //

The Supreme Being has eyes with lashes like the tail-feathers of a bull, beautiful as the splendor of a blue lotus; his lovely face is graced by a pure white ūrṇā-hair between the brows; his head is crowned with an uṣṇīṣa, and his skin is exceedingly fine, radiant, and golden-hued. // 23 //
Each hair on his body grows singly, is soft, points upward, curls to the right, and is exceedingly fine;
his hair is like the pure jewel of great sapphire, and his physical form possesses the luster of a banyan tree in full bloom. // 24 //

With a firm physical form possessing the strength of Nārāyaṇa, the peerless Great Seer Samantabhadra bears these thirty-two marks of a lord of men, which the Teacher proclaims as being of immeasurable splendor. (25)
"Like the moon in water":
just as people perceive the splendor of the moon in a cloudless sky and in a vast lake of dark autumnal waters;
Within the circles of the perfectly awakened ones, the hosts of those sons of the Victorious One behold the sovereign majesty of the All-pervading Lord. // 26 //

Thus, these ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—summarized as one—constitute sixty-four qualities.
These sixty-four qualities, along with their respective causes, should be understood individually and in their proper order, following the *Ratnasūtra*. (27)

Indeed, the detailed analysis and exposition of these sixty-four qualities of a Tathāgata, exactly as they were enumerated above, should be understood according to their sequence by following the *Ratnadārikā-sūtra*.

Furthermore, regarding the fourfold illustrations—the diamond, the lion, the sky, and the moon—cited respectively for these points, their summarized meaning should be understood through twelve verses:
"Because of being piercing, free from dejection, absolute, and effortless..."
It is like the example of a clear mirror, the moon, the sky, and a lion made of vajra. // 28 //

By means of the six, three, and one [stages] of power and so forth, respectively, there is the extraction of all objects of knowledge, the attainment of meditative absorption, and the stains along with their latent predispositions. // 29 //
Because it cannot be split, altered, or cut—like armor, a wall, or a tree—the Sage’s strength is like a diamond (vajra), being heavy, substantial, firm, and indivisible. (30)
Why is it the Guru? Because it is the essence. Why is it the essence? Because it is firm. Why is it firm? Because it is indivisible. And because of its indivisibility, it is like a vajra. // 31 //
Due to fearlessness, lack of attachment, steadfastness, and the perfection of valor,
the lion among sages possesses the absence of timidity amidst the assemblies of followers, just like a lion.

Possessing all supernormal knowledges, he dwells established in his own state, free from fear from any quarter; for he has no expectations even toward pure beings, seeing himself as unequal to them. (33)
He is steadfast because his mind is constantly concentrated upon all phenomena;
he is courageous because he has transcended the ground of the dwelling-place of supreme ignorance. (34)
Due to the progressive subtlety of the intellect among worldly beings, śrāvakas, those who practice exclusively, the wise, and the self-arisen ones, there is a fivefold illustration. (35)
Because they are the source of sustenance for the entire world, they are like earth, water, fire, and air;
because their characteristics transcend both the mundane and the supramundane, they resemble space.
These thirty-two qualities are manifested by the Dharma-body; they are inseparable from it, like the radiance, color, and shape of a precious jewel. // 37 //

The thirty-two marks upon the body are qualities that bring delight to those who behold them; they reside in the two form-bodies: the transformation-body and the enjoyment-body of the Dharma. // 38 //
In this world and likewise in the mandala of the Victor, the pure vision of those who are far from or near to purification is twofold, like the reflection of the moon in water or in the sky. (39)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Chapter on Qualities," in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, the treatise on the supreme jewel of the Mahāyāna.
(Rgv 98) Chapter Four:
The stainless qualities of the Buddha have been explained.
That activity is now to be explained as the "activity of a Jina.
Furthermore, it proceeds briefly from two sources: through effortlessness (*anābhoga*) and through non-cessation (*apraśrabdhi*).
Immediately following, there are two verses concerning the effortless and unceasing work of a Buddha.

In the realm of those to be trained, in the means of training, in the act of training those to be trained, and in going to their respective places and times—the activity of the All-pervading One occurs eternally and indeed effortlessly. // 1 //
Having fully accomplished the vehicle, which contains within its own womb the jewels of knowledge and the multitude of supreme qualities;

and having perceived that Buddhahood— which resembles the vast, infinite, and centerless sky illuminated by the sunbeams of merit and wisdom— is present without distinction in all sentient beings as a treasury of stainless qualities.
The compassion of the Victors, having become like the wind, disperses the cloud-net of afflictions and the knowable. // 2 //
The summarized meaning of these two [verses] should be understood through two and eight verses respectively:

"In whatever way, by whatever means, to whatever extent, and at whatever time the disciplinary action is performed, because there is no arising of conceptual differentiation regarding that, the Sage is always effortless. (3)
For whichever disciple, by whichever manifold means, whatever act of conversion occurs, wherever and whenever—that is, in those respective places and times. // 4 //
Through non-conceptualization regarding the departure [from saṃsāra], its support, its fruit, its appropriation, its recurrence, and the condition for its cessation. // 5 //
The ten stages are the departure; their cause is the two accumulations;
their fruit is supreme enlightenment; and the embrace of sentient beings is the essence of enlightenment. (6)
Its obscuration consists of the limitless latencies of primary and secondary afflictions;
compassion is the cause for their total eradication, existing at all times. (7)
These six bases should be understood in their respective order, like the great ocean, the sun, space, a treasure, a cloud, and the wind. (8)
Because it possesses the jewels of the qualities of the water of knowledge, the Supreme Vehicle is like the ocean;
because it is the source of sustenance for all sentient beings, the two accumulations are like the sun. (9)
Because it is vast, infinite, and without middle, awakening is like the element of space;
because it is the true nature of a perfectly awakened Buddha, the realm of sentient beings is like a treasure-trove. (10)
Because adventitious [defilements] do not pervade [the mind] completely, its affliction is like a mass of clouds;
because they are driven away by the presence of [antidotes], it is like wind arising from compassion. // 11 //

Because of their departure through the welfare of others, because of their vision of the equality of self and sentient beings, and because their task remains unfinished, their activity does not cease until the end of existence. // 12 //

Regarding what has been said— that Buddhahood is characterized by non-arising and non-cessation— how is it that from this unconditioned Buddhahood, which is characterized by non-functioning, the non-conceptual activity of a Buddha proceeds effortlessly and without cessation as long as the world exists?

With reference to the nature of the Buddha’s majesty, there is a verse concerning his majesty, intended to generate faith in the inconceivable domain of the Buddhas among those who have conceived doubts and uncertainties.
The Tathāgata is like Śakra’s drum, like a cloud, like Brahmā, like the sun, like a jewel, like an echo, and like space and the earth. (13)
Indeed, for this verse which serves as the locus of the sutra, a detailed analytical exposition should be understood according to its sequence from the remainder of the treatise.
Regarding the phrase "because it is like the reflection of Śakra": suppose this surface of the earth were made of pure lapis lazuli.
Because of its transparency, the Lord of the Gods, together with the hosts of Apsarases, would be visible there.
The Vaijayanta palace, the other celestial dwellers, their variegated celestial chariots, and those divine manifestations—[all these were seen]. (15)
Then the multitudes of women and men dwelling upon the surface of the earth, having beheld that manifestation, shall make such a prayer: (16)
This very day, or before long, may we thus become lords of the thirty gods; and having undertaken what is wholesome, may we abide for the sake of attaining that state. (17)
Even though they do not recognize that "this is a mere appearance," by that pure karma, they shall pass away from this earth and be reborn in the celestial realms.
That appearance is utterly non-conceptual and effortless;
and thus it would be present upon the earth for the sake of a great purpose. (19)

In the same way, within their own minds—which are stainless through faith and the like, and cultivated by the qualities of faith and so forth—sentient beings perceive the Perfectly Awakened One as a reflection. (20)
Endowed with the primary and secondary marks, performing various modes of deportment—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. (21)
He who proclaims the auspicious Dharma, who remains silent in meditative absorption, and who displays manifold miracles, the one of great splendor— (22)
And having seen him, they apply themselves to the state of Buddhahood, filled with longing;
and by undertaking its cause, they attain the desired state. (23)
That manifestation is utterly free from conceptual construction and devoid of activity;
yet, it is thus present in the worlds for the sake of a great purpose.
Ordinary beings do not realize that "this is a mere reflection of their own minds," yet for them, the vision of that image is not without fruit. (25)
For, having relied upon that vision, those who abide in this system gradually behold the Middle Way—the body of the true Dharma—with the eye of primordial wisdom. (26)

If there were a vast expanse, entirely free from uneven places, intermediate gaps, and impurities, as clear and bright as lapis lazuli, possessing the qualities of a stainless gem, glorious and level; because of its purity, the reflection of the abode of the Lord of Gods— the realm of the Maruts belonging to Mahendra— would appear therein.
It would arise gradually through the departure of the qualities of the earth, and it would again go to its destruction. // 27 //

In order to attain that state, groups of men and women, with focused minds, should be intent on giving alms and other offerings, observing fasts, vows, and restraints, and scatter flowers and the like,
so that the reflection of the Lord of Sages may be perceived in a mind as clear as lapis lazuli.
In the same way, the sons of the Conqueror, with joyful minds, produce various [virtuous qualities]. // 28 //

Just as the reflection of the body of the Lord of Gods appears upon the pure surface of lapis lazuli, so too does the reflection of the body of the Lord of Munis appear upon the pure surface of the minds of sentient beings. // 29 //
Arising from the lineage of the manifestation of one's own mind—which is pure and radiant despite the appearance and disappearance of reflected images—it proceeds throughout the world.
Just as a reflection appears among people, so too should one perceive it as being neither existent nor non-existent. // 30 //
"Like the celestial drum":
just as in heaven, due to the power of previous virtuous deeds, there exists for the gods a state that is free from effort, location, mental form, and conceptual construction. (31)
The divine drum repeatedly exhorts all the heedless gods with the sounds of impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and peace. (32)

Thus, the All-pervading One, having pervaded the entire world with the very voice of a Buddha, teaches the Dharma to those who are capable, even though he is himself devoid of effort and the like. // 33 //
Just as the sound of divine drums in heaven arises for the gods through their own karma, so too does the teaching of the Dharma by the Sage arise in the world through his own karma;
that sound, being devoid of effort, location, body, and mind, brings about peace.
Just as that is so, even so, that Dharma consisting of the fourfold [truth] brings about peace. // 34 //

Just as in the city of the gods, the sound arising from the cause of the drum’s resonance dispels the play of conquering the forces of the asuras during the turmoil of battle and bestows fearlessness; so too,
in the practice of the supreme path, it pacifies and subdues the suffering of the afflictions within sentient beings.
Likewise, it is declared in the world that [the fruits] arise from causes such as the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and the formless attainments (ārūpya). // 35 //
Why is it that here only the Dharma drum is treated as the subject, and not the other types of divine musical instruments?
For even those [instruments] produce sounds that are delightful to the divine ear without being struck, by the power of the virtuous karma previously performed by the celestial beings.
Nevertheless, they differ from the voice of the Tathāgata in four respects regarding their qualities.
What, then, is that?
It is as follows: partiality, lack of benefit, lack of happiness, and lack of definitive emergence.
Furthermore, the drum of the Dharma is described by its non-partiality, because it exhorts the entire host of heedless gods and because it does not allow that time to pass.

Its quality of being beneficial (*hitatva*) is elucidated by its protection from the fear of affliction caused by enemies such as the *asuras* and others, and by its application to heedfulness (*apramāda*). Its quality of being pleasant (*sukhatva*) is elucidated by its separation from the pleasure of delighting in unwholesome desires and by its bringing about the pleasure of delighting in the garden of the Dharma (*dharmārāma*).

Its quality of leading to liberation (*nairyāṇikatva*) is elucidated by the utterance of the terms "impermanent," "suffering," "empty," and "non-self," and by its effecting the pacification of all calamities and distresses.
In brief, by these four aspects, the mandala of the Buddha’s voice is distinguished through its similarity to the drum of the Dharma.
This is the verse concerning the distinction of the mandala of the Buddha’s voice:
It is for all people, it brings benefit and happiness, and it is endowed with the three miracles.
Therefore, the voice of the Sage excels that of divine musical instruments. // 36 //
Indeed, it should be understood that a concise explanation of these four aspects is given by means of four verses, respectively:
The great sounds of celestial drums do not reach the ears of those dwelling on the earth;
yet the sound of the drum of the Perfectly Awakened One reaches those in the world who have fallen into the depths of saṃsāra. (37)
In heaven, many tens of millions of musical instruments of the immortals resound to increase the fire of desire;
but the single voice of those whose nature is compassion is directed toward extinguishing the causes of the fire of suffering.

In heaven, the sounds of musical instruments are beautiful and pleasing, yet they serve as causes for the increase of mental agitation; whereas the speech of the great-souled Tathāgatas expresses the state of bestowing the mind upon meditative concentration. (39)

In brief, whatever cause of happiness exists in heaven, on earth, or even in infinite world-systems—that which illuminates and pervades the entire world—has also been proclaimed by resorting to this proclamation. (40)
The miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) is indicated as the pervading of the entirety of the world-systems in the ten directions through the transformation of the body.

The miracle of mind-reading (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*) is the illumination of the dense thicket of the mental conduct of all sentient beings included therein by means of the knowledge of others' minds (*cetaḥparyāya-jñāna*). The miracle of instruction (*anuśāsanā-prātihārya*) is that which instructs by means of the utterance of vocal sounds, beginning with the path leading to liberation, through advice and precepts.

Thus, although the circle of the Buddha’s voice has an unimpeded course and exists as something unlimited like the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*), the fact that the perception of every sound does not arise everywhere is not due to any fault in the circle of the Buddha’s voice.
This verse is intended to show that those who do not understand this have committed a fault against themselves.
Just as one who lacks a physical ear does not perceive subtle sounds,
nor do they all come within the range of hearing even for one with divine ears,
so too is the Dharma subtle, being the object of the most refined wisdom.
But for some whose minds are not distracted, it reaches the path of their hearing.
Regarding the phrase "like a cloud":
just as in the rainy season a cloud pours down rain upon the earth.
The effortless accumulation of water is the sign of an abundant harvest. // 42 //
In the same way, the Victor pours down the rain of the true Dharma from the cloud of compassion, without conceptual construction, upon the crops of virtue in the world. (43)

Just as in the world clouds rain down water produced by the wind when the paths of wholesome action prevail, so too does the cloud that is the Buddha pour down the rain of the true Dharma for the sake of increasing the roots of virtue in the world through the wind of compassion. (44)

The cloud-like Lord of Sages, who carries the rain of wisdom and compassion amidst the realms of existence, who dwells in the expanse of the sky free from attachment to the conditioned and the unconditioned, and who contains within him the pure waters of meditative concentration and mnemonic power, is the cause for the harvest of auspicious merit.
Regarding the diversity of receptacles:

just as water that is cool, sweet, clear, soft, and light becomes exceedingly rich in flavor through contact with saline and other locations on the earth, so too does it become liberated from its original state through the emergence of those [qualities].

Just as rain consisting of the water of the Noble Eightfold Path, released from the womb of the vast cloud of compassion, assumes many kinds of flavors according to the differences in the receptacles and locations of the streams, so it is with respect to living beings.

Regarding their engagement without regard [for others]: there are three classes of people—those who have faith in the supreme vehicle, those who are indifferent, and those who are hostile; they are like humans, cātaka birds, and pretas, respectively. (47)
At the end of summer, when clouds are absent, men cannot travel through the sky; during the rains, birds suffer from the falling of excessive downpours;
and likewise, when the rain-clouds of the Dharma—the waters of compassion—do not manifest or arise, hungry ghosts (pretas) are tormented by the falling of [the rain of] suffering.
And for one who desires the Dharma and is not obstructed by the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) in the world, that very same analogy applies. 48.
Just as a rain-cloud does not disregard those traveling through mountainous regions or among tiny living beings when it pours down large drops like thunderbolts or strikes with lightning and fire,
so too the cloud of wisdom and compassion, through subtle and gross methods, skillful means, and procedures, [acts for the benefit of all].
In the same way, one does not regard the latent tendencies of views residing within the afflictions in any manner whatsoever. // 49 //
In the extinguishing of the fire of suffering,

saṃsāra consists of births and deaths without beginning or end; within that wandering, the path is fivefold, and on that fivefold way there is no happiness, just as there is no fragrance in excrement.
That suffering is certain to arise from contact with fire, weapons, cold, alkaline substances, and the like;
and to pacify it, the Cloud of Compassion pours down the great rain of the True Dharma.

Because they understand that there is the suffering of death and decline among the gods, the wise do not desire even the highest sovereignty over gods and humans— the suffering of seeking [rebirth] among men;
and this is due to their wisdom, which follows from faith in the Tathāgata’s teaching.
Because of the thorough contemplation through the knowledge that "this is suffering," "this is the cause," and "this is cessation. // 51 //

Disease is to be known, the cause of disease is to be abandoned, health is to be attained, and medicine is to be used; likewise, suffering is to be known, its cause is to be abandoned, its cessation is to be touched [realized], and the path is to be cultivated. // 52 //
"Like Mahābrahmā": Just as Brahmā, without wavering from his sublime state, manifests his appearance effortlessly throughout all the celestial abodes; // 53 //
In the same way, the Sage, without moving from the *dharmakāya*, appears to those who are worthy through effortless emanations throughout all realms.
Just as Brahmā, though never departing from his celestial palace, constantly enters the realm of desire.
The gods behold him, and that vision of theirs removes their attachment to sense-objects;
likewise, the Sugata does not move from the body of the True Dharma in all worlds, yet those who are worthy behold him, and that vision of theirs perpetually removes every stain. (55)
Due to the power of his own former vows and through the auspicious influence of the hosts of gods,
the Self-Existent One likewise manifests by means of an emanation body without effort, just as Brahmā attains his radiance effortlessly.
In the state of non-appearance, [he manifests] his passing away, his entry into the womb, his birth, his entering the father’s house,
his wandering through pleasure-gardens and forests, and his subduing of Māra.
Having demonstrated the attainment of great enlightenment and the guidance upon the path to the city of peace, the Sage does not come within the range of vision of those who lack merit. // 57 //
"Like the sun":

Just as when the sun shines, at one and the same time there is the awakening of the multitude of lotuses and the closing of the night-lilies; and just as the sun is without conceptual construction regarding the production of qualities or defects in the lotuses, so too is the Noble Sun here. (58)
The realm of sentient beings is twofold: those who are not to be trained and those who are to be trained.
With reference to those who are to be trained, there is the likeness to a lotus and the likeness to a vessel of clear water.
Just as the sun, being free from conceptual construction, [awakens] the lotuses with its rays;
It awakens by means of some [beings] who are already liberated, and it brings others also to maturity. // 59 //
In this way, the sun-like Tathāgata, free from conceptual construction, proceeds by means of the rays of the true Dharma toward the lotuses of those beings who are to be trained.
Risen into the sky of the seat of awakening through his body of dharma and his physical form, the sun of the Omniscient One pervades the world with the rays of his primordial wisdom. (61)
For, wherever the vessel of those to be trained is pure, the reflection of the immeasurable sun of the Sugata arises all at once.

Thus, even though the Buddhas are free from conceptual construction, with respect to the sequence of their engagement in seeing and teaching for the threefold assembly of sentient beings, they possess a resemblance to a mountain: "While the sun of the Buddha constantly radiates everywhere across the sky-like expanse of the *dharmadhātu*, its descent upon the mountains of those to be trained occurs according to what is appropriate."
Just as the seven-horsed sun, having risen here and illuminated the world on all sides with its extended thousand rays,
shines successively upon the highest, middle, and lowest mountains; even so, the Sun of the Jina shines successively upon the multitude of sentient beings.
Regarding the specific qualities of the circle of light:
the sun does not possess the quality of pervading the sky of all buddha-fields,
nor does it possess the manifestation of the objects of knowledge within the dense darkness of the gloom of ignorance.
Those whose nature is compassion illuminate the world with emanations of light rays of various colors arising from each individual pore, revealing the objects that are to be known. // 65 //
At the time of the Buddhas' entry into the city, those who are deprived of sight behold [the truth] and, through that vision, find the cessation of the web of misfortunes;
yet those blinded by delusion remain within the ocean of existence, shrouded by the darkness of false views.
Those whose intellects are illuminated by the light of the Buddha-sun behold the previously unseen state.

Like a wish-fulfilling gem: although it is free from conceptual construction, it simultaneously fulfills all the intentions of those situated within its range, just as a wish-fulfilling gem does individually. // 67 //
In the same way, having gathered around the wish-fulfilling gem that is the Buddha, those with diverse inclinations hear the manifold nature of reality; yet he does not conceptualize them.

Just as a wish-fulfilling jewel effortlessly bestows upon others whatever desired wealth they conceive in their thoughts, so too does the Sage, without effort, constantly attend to the welfare of others according to their needs until the end of existence. (69)
"Tathāgatas are beings whose attainment is difficult to find. In this world, the acquisition of a pure jewel is likewise extremely rare,
for people long for that which has gone into the ocean or resides in the netherworld (pātāla).

Just as that [jewel] is not easily obtained, so too should it be known that the vision of the Tathāgata is extremely difficult to find in this world when the mind is seized by various afflictions. (70)
Like the sound of an echo: Just as the sound of an echo arises from the cognition of another, it is free from conceptual construction and effortless, abiding neither within nor without. (71)
In the same way, the speech of the Tathāgata arises from the communication of others;
it is free from conceptual construction and effortless, abiding neither within nor without. // 72 //
"Like space":
it is without anything, without appearance, without support, and without basis;
it transcends the path of the eye, being formless and invisible. (73)
Just as depressions and elevations are seen in the sky, yet they do not exist there in that way;
so too, everything is seen even among the Buddhas, yet it does not exist there in that way. // 74 //
"Like the earth":
Just as all trees, depending upon the earth which is free from conceptual construction, attain growth, development, and expansion; // 75 //
In this way, upon the ground of the Perfectly Awakened One, which is entirely free from conceptual construction, the roots of virtue of the world indeed proceed toward growth. (76)
The summarized meaning of the examples is as follows:
"Since no one is ever seen performing an action without effort, these nine illustrations have been taught in order to sever the doubts of those to be trained. (77)
The purpose of that sūtra is illuminated by its very name, wherein these nine similes are revealed in detail. (78)
Adorned with the light of vast wisdom arising from hearing this, the wise quickly enter the entire domain of the Buddhas. (79)
For this purpose, nine examples—such as the reflection of Śakra and lapis lazuli—are cited therein; from them, the summarized meaning (piṇḍārtha) is to be understood. (80)
For those whose nature is compassion, there are vision, teaching, pervasiveness, transformation, the emergence of knowledge, the secrets of mind, speech, and body, and attainment. (81)
Their cognitions, free from conceptual construction, are stilled in all effort and movement, like the rising of the reflection of Śakra in a stainless lapis lazuli gem. (82)
The thesis is the state of tranquility regarding the enjoyment [of objects]; the reason is the non-conceptuality of the intellect;
the example is the reflection of Śakra and so forth, for the sake of successfully establishing the subject matter at hand. (83)
And this is the subject at hand here: the ninefold [activity] beginning with vision proceeds effortlessly after the Teacher’s death, throughout his births and disappearances. (84)
With reference to this very meaning, there are four verses in the *Saṃgraha-udāharaṇa*:

He who, like Śakra, like a drum, like a cloud, like Brahmā, the sun, the wish-fulfilling gem, the king of jewels, like an echo, space, and the earth, performs the welfare of others without effort throughout the course of existence—he is the knower of yoga. (85)
The Great Teacher, who manifests like the reflection of the jewels of the Lord of Gods, whose voice is like a drum,
the pervasive one whose mandala is the clouds of great wisdom and compassion, radiates throughout the infinite world as far as the peak of existence.
From the stainless state, like Brahmā, he does not fall from his station, yet through emanations he appears in manifold ways;
like the sun, his radiance issues forth from wisdom, and his mind is a pure wish-fulfilling gem. (87)
The voice of the Victors is like an echo, uttered without syllables;
their body is like the sky, pervasive, formless, and eternal;
they are like the earth for all the medicinal herbs of pure qualities.
The stage of Buddhahood is the universal abode for the world here. // 88 //
Furthermore, how is it illustrated by this presentation of examples that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though eternally unarisen and unceasing,
are nevertheless seen arising and ceasing, and that throughout the entire world their Buddha-activity proceeds without effort and without interruption?
"Purity in the mind, like lapis lazuli, is the cause for the vision of the Buddha."
Its purification is the growth of the faculty of faith that cannot be taken away. // 89 //

Because of the arising and passing away of what is auspicious, there is the arising and passing away of the reflected image; yet the Sage does not arise nor pass away from the Dharmakāya, like Śakra [from his palace]. (90)
Thus, seeing that "the task is accomplished without effort," [the Buddha] engages in such activities as teaching the Dharma;
this proceeds from the Dharmakāya, which is without arising or cessation, for as long as existence endures. // 91 //

This is the summarized meaning of these similes; furthermore, the sequence has been stated by means of the latter [simile] as a rebuttal to the objection regarding the dissimilarity of the former. (92)
Buddhahood is like a reflected image, yet it is not like that; it is like the divine drum, yet it is not like that either, for it does not fail to accomplish the welfare of beings in every way. (93)
It is like a great cloud, yet not like the seed of a merchant's caravan; it is like Mahābrahmā, yet not one who brings about ultimate ripening. // 94 //
Like the solar disc, it likewise does not remove darkness absolutely;
like the wish-fulfilling gem, it likewise does not have a difficult arising. // 95 //
Like an echo, it does not arise from conditions;
like space, it is not a locus for purity. // 96 //
Resembling the circle of the earth because it serves as its foundation and support, it is the source of all mundane and supramundane excellence of virtue for the world. (97)

Having attained the awakening of the Buddhas through the arising of the supramundane path, there occurs the production of the paths of white karma, the meditative absorptions, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments. // 98 //

Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Section on the Performance of the Tathāgata’s Deeds, in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, the Treatise on the Ultimate Continuum of the Mahāyāna, according to the commentary summarizing the meaning of the verses.
(Rgv 115) 5. The Fifth Chapter:
Thereafter, there are six verses concerning the benefits of resolute belief for those who possess resolute belief in these very places as they have been described.
The Buddha-element, the awakening of the Buddha, the Buddha-qualities, and the Buddha-activity—this is the domain of the Leaders, inconceivable even to pure beings. (1)
In this regard, the wise person whose intellect is resolved upon the Victor becomes a vessel for a multitude of virtues;
through the application of a longing for inconceivable qualities, they surpass the production of merit of all sentient beings. // 2 //

Suppose someone, seeking awakening, were to offer every day to the Lords of Dharma Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms of a Buddha-field, adorned with jewels and made of gold; and suppose there were another who,
having heard even a single word from this [teaching], upon hearing it, should have faith— this latter person would [surpass the former].
Therefore, one would acquire much more merit than from the excellence consisting of giving. // 3 //
The wise person who, desiring unsurpassed enlightenment, might for many eons protect stainless morality of body, speech, and mind with effortless spontaneity;
and another who might hear even a single word from this [teaching] and, having heard it, develop faith— [the latter would generate greater merit].
Therefore, one should acquire merit far greater than that consisting of virtuous conduct. // 4 //
One who meditates here upon this meditation— which extinguishes the fire of affliction in the three worlds,
which has reached the perfection of the divine Brahma-abodes, and which does not fall away from the means to perfect enlightenment—
and another who might hear even a single word from this and, having heard it, develop faith in it; [of these two, the latter is superior].
Therefore, one shall obtain much greater merit than that which consists of meditative absorption. // 5 //

Generosity brings about wealth; morality leads to heaven; meditation results in the destruction of the afflictions; and wisdom is the abandonment of all afflictive and cognitive obscurations. Therefore, hearing this [teaching] is the most excellent cause for that [wisdom]. (6)
The summarized meaning of these verses is to be understood through the following nine verses:

"In this fourfold object of the Victor’s knowledge as it has been described—namely, the basis, its transformation, its qualities, and the accomplishment of the welfare [of beings]—[the following applies]. (7)
Through the conviction that [the Buddha] possesses wisdom, existence, power, and qualities, one quickly attains the fitness for reaching the state of a Tathāgata. // 8 //
This inconceivable realm exists; it can be attained by those like me, and it possesses such qualities—this is understood through faith and resolute conviction. (9)
The bodhicitta of this person becomes a vessel for qualities such as aspiration, vigor, mindfulness, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and it remains constantly established before him. (10)
Because that mind is present before him, the Son of the Conqueror becomes irreversible and attains the fulfillment and purification of the perfection of merit. // 11 //

The five perfections are merit; they are threefold because of the non-conceptualization regarding them. Their fulfillment is their complete purification through the abandonment of their opposites. // 12 //
Generosity is known as merit consisting of generosity; ethical discipline is known as merit consisting of ethical discipline;
patience and meditative concentration consist of cultivation; while vigor is all-pervasive. (13)

The conceptualization of the three spheres is considered the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); that which consists of the opposing factors such as stinginess and so forth is considered the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*). // 14 //
And there is no cause for this abandonment other than wisdom; therefore, wisdom is supreme, and its root is learning. Consequently, learning is paramount. (15)

Thus, this has been set forth solely for the sake of self-purification by relying upon authoritative scripture and reasoning; and also for the benefit of those who are endowed with intelligence, resolute faith, and the perfection of wholesome qualities. (16)

Just as those with sight perceive [forms] by depending on lamps, lightning, jewels, the moon, and the sun, so too has this been proclaimed by depending upon the Sage, who illuminates the Dharma of great significance through his inspired eloquence. (17)

That speech which is meaningful, endowed with the word "Dharma," which uproots the afflictions of the three realms, and which demonstrates the benefits of peace—that is said to be the word of the Sages; anything otherwise is the opposite.

Whatever has been spoken by those with undistracted minds, pointing toward the Teacher, the sole Victor, and which accords with the path of the equipment for attaining liberation—even that one should receive upon the crown of one's head as if it were the word of a Sage. (19)
Since there is no one anywhere in this world more wise than the Jina,
who is omniscient and knows the entirety of the supreme reality exactly as it is— none other than he—
therefore, that sutra which has been personally set forth by the Sage must not be rejected.
For even that would constitute an obstruction to the True Dharma, O Sage, because it creates a division in the teaching. // 20 //
That they revile the noble ones and despise the Dharma taught by them— all that is a defilement produced by the views of dogmatic attachment belonging to those of deluded mind.
Therefore, one’s intellect should not be fixed upon that which is stained by the view of dogmatic attachment.
A clean cloth takes on the transformation of dye, but one stained with oil and mud does not. // 21 //

Due to dullness of intellect, lack of resolute faith and virtuous qualities, reliance on false pride, being obscured by the ruin of the true Dharma, grasping at the provisional meaning as the ultimate reality,
excessive greed, the power of [wrong] views, and serving those who are enemies of the Dharma;
And having offended those who uphold the Dharma, those of inferior inclination revile the teachings of the Arhats. // 22 //

The wise should not fear fire, nor poison, nor snakes, nor executioners, nor even thunderbolts as much as they should fear the injury to the profound Dharma; for fire, serpents, enemies, and the lightning-fire can only cause the loss of life, but not the destruction of the Dharma.
For that reason, one should not again go to the most terrifying state of the Avīci hell. // 23 //
Even for that man who, having repeatedly served evil friends, harbors malice toward the Buddha,
commits the murder of mother, father, or an Arhat, or causes a schism in the Sangha— the foremost of assemblies—
there may yet be liberation from that [sin] before long through the contemplation of the meaning of the Dharma.
But for one whose mind is hostile toward the Dharma, how can there be liberation? // 24 //
By whatever merit I have acquired through correctly explaining the seven points of meaning— the jewels, the stainless realm of purification, enlightenment, the qualities, and the activity—
may these people behold the Sage Amitāyus, who possesses infinite radiance.
And having seen [this], through the arising of the stainless eye of Dharma, one shall attain supreme enlightenment. // 25 //
The summarized meaning of these ten verses should be understood through three [concluding] verses:
"From what source, for what cause, in what manner, and what was illustrated—this, along with its natural outflow as a fruit, is elucidated by four verses. (26)
The means for self-protection is explained by two verses, and the cause and effect of injury by one verse; thus [the topic] is elucidated by these three stanzas. // 27 //
In brief, the patient acceptance of the circle of saṃsāra and the attainment of awakening are shown at the end as the two-fold fruit of the discourse on the meaning of the Dharma. // 28 //
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Benefits," in the *Ratnagotravibhāga Mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra*, according to the commentary summarizing the meaning of the verses. // 5 //
